title: INTERNAL Error `physical_index != DConstants::INVALID_INDEX` in propagate_get.cpp when statistics fold a pushed-down filter's column away
body:
### What happens?

On current `main`, built with assertions enabled (`make relassert`), this valid query fails with an assertion
INTERNAL error instead of returning an empty result. The v1.5.6 release returns 0 rows. After the error the database
instance is invalidated.

## SQL

```sql
CREATE TABLE t0(c0 INTEGER);
SELECT 1 FROM t0 WHERE (c0 IS NULL) IN (NULL, true) AND (c0 = 1 OR 0 IN (SELECT 0));
```

## Observed (validated 2026-10-18)

**main 16917f94f9e0 (v2.1.0-dev89189), `make relassert`**
```
INTERNAL Error: Assertion triggered in file "src/optimizer/statistics/operator/../../../../../../src/optimizer/statistics/operator/propagate_get.cpp" on line 37: physical_index != DConstants::INVALID_INDEX
```

**v2.0-cyanoptera 804b3f2070e3 (v2.0.0-dev88581), `make relassert`**
```
INTERNAL Error: Assertion triggered in file "src/optimizer/statistics/operator/../../../../../../src/optimizer/statistics/operator/propagate_get.cpp" on line 37: physical_index != DConstants::INVALID_INDEX
```

**v1.5.6 release CLI (069cc9f9b5)**
```
┌────────┐
│   1    │
│ int32  │
└────────┘
  0 rows
```


### To Reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE t0(c0 INTEGER);
SELECT 1 FROM t0 WHERE (c0 IS NULL) IN (NULL, true) AND (c0 = 1 OR 0 IN (SELECT 0));
```

### OS:

macOS 26 (aarch64)

### DuckDB Version:

main 16917f94f9e0 (v2.1.0-dev89189), `make relassert`

### DuckDB Client:

CLI

### Hardware:

_No response_

### Full Name:

Alperen Keles

### Affiliation:

Datadog

- [x] Yes, I have

### Did you include all code required to reproduce the issue?

- [x] Yes, I have

### Did you include all relevant data sets for reproducing the issue?

Yes
fix_test_text:
--- test/optimizer/statistics/statistics_table_filter_column_folded.test
@@ -2,11 +2,15 @@
 # description: A table filter keeps referencing its column when statistics fold the column away
 # group: [statistics]
 
-# the filter on c0 is folded into a constant by statistics propagation, but the table filter has to keep
-# referencing the column it filters on - otherwise the next statistics propagation pass cannot find the column
+# Empty-table statistics must not leave a column-free filter for the next propagation pass.
 statement ok
 CREATE TABLE t0(c0 INTEGER);
 
+query I
+SELECT 1 FROM t0 WHERE (c0 IS NULL) IN (NULL, true) AND (c0 = 1 OR 0 IN (SELECT 0));
+----
+
+# Nullable input must still return the matching row.
 statement ok
 INSERT INTO t0 VALUES (NULL), (5), (1);
 
@@ -57,7 +61,7 @@ EXPLAIN SELECT 1 FROM t1 WHERE (c0 IS NULL) IN (NULL, true) AND (c0 = 1 OR 0 IN
 ----
 logical_opt	<REGEX>:.*\(c0 IS NULL\) IN \(NULL::BOOLEAN, true\).*
 
-# a filter that is folded into a constant no longer filters on the column, so it is removed from the scan
+# Statistics can still prune a scan when its filter cannot match any row.
 query II
 EXPLAIN SELECT 1 FROM t1 WHERE c0 IS NULL;
 ----

title: INTERNAL Error “Vector::Reference used on vector of different type” filtering a STRUCT child with OFFSET with v2
body:
### What happens?

This works on 1.5.x, filtering on a child field of a `STRUCT` column fails with an internal error as soon as the query has an OFFSET, OFFSET 0 included. The same query without OFFSET works, and both work on 1.5.5. The error invalidates the database, so every later query on the connection fails with “database has been invalidated because of a previous fatal error”.

```
INTERNAL Error: Vector::Reference used on vector of different type (source STRUCT(xmin DOUBLE, xmax DOUBLE, ymin DOUBLE, ymax DOUBLE) referenced DOUBLE)
```

The file is the Overture Maps divisions release 2026-09-23.1: a single public file of 4,688,229 rows in 256 row groups, written by parquet-cpp-arrow 17.0.0. bbox is an optional struct of four optional doubles, with statistics on each child. 
I couldn't reproduce it with small files written by DuckDB with the same struct and predicate. It looks like close to #26156, with the same message and a struct child filter, closed early October. Here neither `union_by_name` nor `hive_partitioning` is needed, and the spatial extension is not loaded.

### To Reproduce

```sql
INSTALL httpfs;
LOAD httpfs;
CREATE SECRET (TYPE s3, REGION 'us-west-2', KEY_ID '', SECRET '');

-- works
SELECT id
FROM read_parquet('s3://overturemaps-us-west-2/release/2026-09-23.1/theme=divisions/type=division/part-00000-8b67a992-99db-52a1-aeb0-1b049a9a125c-c000.zstd.parquet')
WHERE bbox.xmin <= 12.8
LIMIT 1;

-- INTERNAL Error
SELECT id
FROM read_parquet('s3://overturemaps-us-west-2/release/2026-09-23.1/theme=divisions/type=division/part-00000-8b67a992-99db-52a1-aeb0-1b049a9a125c-c000.zstd.parquet')
WHERE bbox.xmin <= 12.8
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 0;
```

The bucket is public. The empty KEY_ID and SECRET make the read unsigned. OFFSET 10 fails the same way, and so does a filter on all four bounds of bbox.

### OS:

macOS 15.6 (arm64); Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu)

### DuckDB Version:

2.0.0

### DuckDB Client:

Python (3.13 on macOS, 3.12 on Linux)

### Hardware:

Apple M1 Max, 64 GB; Fly.io shared-cpu-1x, 2 GB

### Full Name:

Francesco Bartoli

### Affiliation:

Geobeyond

title: ManualVuln1 Virtual column ID used as index into returned_types in CreateLHSGet
body:
### What happens?

In `src/optimizer/late_materialization_helper.cpp` line 23-24, the `CreateLHSGet` function iterates over all pushed-down table filters on a `LogicalGet` and looks up the column type via `rhs.returned_types[col_idx]`.
The variable `col_idx` is obtained via `column_ids[filter_entry.GetIndex()].GetPrimaryIndex()`.
When the filter targets a virtual column (such as the `filename` column in a multi-file Parquet scan), `col_idx` carries a virtual column identifier with a value >= `VIRTUAL_COLUMN_START` (2^63 = 9223372036854775808).
No `IsVirtualColumn(col_idx)` guard is present before the `returned_types[col_idx]` access.
DuckDB's safe-vector bounds check therefore fires and throws `InternalException("Attempted to access index -9223372036854775808 within vector of size 4")`, aborting the query with "This error signals an assertion failure within DuckDB."

The violated invariant is: every access to `returned_types[col_id]` must be preceded by a check that `!IsVirtualColumn(col_id)`, because virtual column IDs lie far outside the size of `returned_types`.

This is the exact same root-cause pattern patched in Entry18: `plan_get.cpp` and `multi_file_column_mapper.cpp` already received `IsVirtualColumn` guards before indexing `returned_types`, but `late_materialization_helper.cpp` was left unpatched.

Late materialization is triggered when: a table function has `late_materialization = true` (Parquet sets this in `extension/parquet/read_single_parquet_file.cpp:523`), the query projects more columns than are required by the sort key and the pushed-down filters, and a TOP-N (`ORDER BY ... LIMIT`) is present.
Adding a `filename` filter (virtual column) satisfies the "pushed-down filter on virtual column" condition.
Using `SELECT *` on a four-column Parquet file while sorting on one column ensures that `required_columns.size() < get.GetColumnIds().size()`, triggering late materialization.
`CreateLHSGet` then reaches the unguarded `returned_types[col_idx]` access with a virtual column ID.


### To Reproduce

Step 1: create the Parquet fixture (run once before step 2).

Run directly via the DuckDB ASAN CLI:

```sql
COPY (SELECT i, i + 1 AS j, i + 2 AS k, -i AS l FROM range(100) t(i)) TO '/tmp/test_entry18.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET)
```

Step 2: trigger the crash.

```sql
SELECT * FROM read_parquet('/tmp/test_entry18.parquet') WHERE filename LIKE '%test_entry18%' ORDER BY j DESC LIMIT 5
```

Trigger output:

```
INTERNAL Error: Attempted to access index -9223372036854775808 within vector of size 4

Stack Trace:

/data/ylwang/Projects/DirectedDB/latesttarget/duckdb/build_asan/duckdb(+0x2ae4c476) [0x60af961c9476]
...

This error signals an assertion failure within DuckDB.
For more information, see https://duckdb.org/docs/current/dev/internal_errors
exit: 1
```

### OS:

Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS, x86_64 (Linux 6.8.0-55-generic)

### DuckDB Version:

v2.0.0-dev87784

### DuckDB Client:

duckdb CLI, ASAN+UBSan instrumented build (built from source)

### Hardware:

_No response_

Yuelin

### Affiliation:

Individual

title: `&&` (`ST_Intersects_Extent`) on CRS-parameterized `GEOMETRY('<crs>')` is not pushed down in conjunctions on 2.0
body:
### What happens?

On DuckDB 2.0 nightlies (`2.0.0.dev2609250715`, `2.0.0.dev2610011535`), a bounding-box filter `g && <geom>` (`ST_Intersects_Extent`) on a CRS-parameterized geometry column (e.g. `GEOMETRY('OGC:CRS84')` or `GEOMETRY('EPSG:4326')`) is not pushed down into the table scan when combined in an `AND` conjunction with `ST_Intersects(g, <geom>)` (or any other potentially throwing predicate). Both filters remain in a `FILTER` operator above the scan, preventing row-group and file pruning across native DuckDB tables, `read_parquet`, and `iceberg_scan`.

In DuckDB 1.5.6, the same query pushes the filters into the scan and prunes row groups and data files.

### To Reproduce

With `spatial` (200,000 points spanning `(0.0, 0.0)` to `(19.9999, 19.9999)` across 2 row groups):

```sql
INSTALL spatial;
LOAD spatial;

CREATE TABLE t AS
SELECT ST_Point(i * 0.0001, i * 0.0001)::GEOMETRY('EPSG:4326') AS g
FROM range(200000) t(i);

-- 1. && alone: pushed down on 2.0 (Row Groups Scanned: 1 / 2, 1 row)
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT count(*) FROM t
WHERE g && ST_Point(0.0002, 0.0002);

-- 2. && AND ST_Intersects: NOT pushed down on 2.0 (Row Groups Scanned: 2 / 2, 200,000 rows)
--    In 1.5.6 this pushes down and scans 1 / 2 row groups.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT count(*) FROM t
WHERE g && ST_Point(0.0002, 0.0002)
  AND ST_Intersects(g, ST_Point(0.0002, 0.0002));

-- 3. Workaround with TRY_CAST: pushed down on 2.0 (Row Groups Scanned: 1 / 2, 1 row)
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT count(*) FROM t
WHERE TRY_CAST(g AS GEOMETRY) && ST_Point(0.0002, 0.0002)
  AND ST_Intersects(g, ST_Point(0.0002, 0.0002));
```

Zero-extension reproduction (using built-in `OGC:CRS84` and any throwing predicate):

```sql
CREATE TABLE t AS
SELECT '1' AS id, ('POINT(' || (i * 0.0001) || ' ' || (i * 0.0001) || ')')::GEOMETRY('OGC:CRS84') AS g
FROM range(200000) t(i);

-- Scans 2 / 2 row groups (200,000 rows) into a Filter operator above the scan on 2.0:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT count(*) FROM t
WHERE g && 'POINT(0.0002 0.0002)'::GEOMETRY
  AND id::INT = 1;
```

### Root Cause

1. `StIntersectsExtentFun::GetFunction()` (`src/function/scalar/geometry/geometry_functions.cpp:203-210`) registers `&&` / `ST_Intersects_Extent` with `(GEOMETRY, GEOMETRY)` and no bind callback to preserve the input CRS, so the binder wraps `g` in `CAST(g AS GEOMETRY)`.
2. In `BoundCastExpression::CastCanThrow` (`src/planner/expression/bound_cast_expression.cpp:271-322`), `source_type == target_type` is `false` for `GEOMETRY('<crs>') -> GEOMETRY`, and `DefaultTryGetMaxLogicalTypeUnchecked(source_type, target_type, max_type)` hits the equal-`LogicalTypeId` fallthrough in `TryGetMaxLogicalTypeInternal` (`src/common/types.cpp:1030`), returning `max_type = source_type`. Thus `max_type != target_type` evaluates to `true`, classifying the no-op `DefaultCasts::ReinterpretCast` (`src/function/cast/geo_casts.cpp:35`) as `CanThrow() == true`.
3. In `FilterPushdown::PushdownGet` (`src/optimizer/pushdown/pushdown_get.cpp:117`), `if (expr.CanThrow() && filters.size() > 1)` skips both `CAST(g AS GEOMETRY) && ...` and `ST_Intersects(...)` (which is also marked `CanThrow() == true`), leaving `get.table_filters` empty.

### Context

Originally encountered via `iceberg_scan` in https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-iceberg/issues/1464 (see also https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-iceberg/pull/1467), since Iceberg V3 geometry columns always carry a CRS (`GEOMETRY('OGC:CRS84')` by default or `GEOMETRY('<crs>')`).
fix_test_text:
--- test/sql/types/geo/geometry_parquet_pushdown.test
@@ -42,3 +42,29 @@ FROM '{TEST_DIR}/output.json' prof,
 WHERE t.type = 'TABLE_SCAN';
 ----
 2
+
+# Combining && on a GEOMETRY('<crs>') column with a fallible predicate should still push down && and prune row groups.
+statement ok
+PRAGMA enable_profiling = 'json';
+
+statement ok
+PRAGMA profiling_output = '{TEST_DIR}/output_multi.json';
+
+statement ok
+SET tracked_metrics = ['operator.type', 'operator.row_groups_scanned', 'operator.total_row_groups_to_scan'];
+
+statement ok
+select * from '{TEST_DIR}/points.parquet' where g && 'POLYGON((10 10, 20 10, 20 20, 10 20, 10 10))'::GEOMETRY and id::VARCHAR::INT >= 0;
+
+statement ok
+PRAGMA disable_profiling;
+
+query I
+SELECT t.row_groups_scanned
+FROM '{TEST_DIR}/output_multi.json' prof,
+     LATERAL unnest(prof.operator) t0(op0),
+     LATERAL unnest(op0.children) t1(op1),
+     LATERAL unnest(op1.children) t2(t)
+WHERE t.type = 'TABLE_SCAN';
+----
+2

title: 2.0 alpha: comparing a CASE/split_part result to a constant fails with "BindBuiltinScalarFunction did not return a BoundFunctionExpression" when the column is NULL in every row
body:
### What happens?

On the 2.0 alpha, a `WHERE` filter that compares a string derived from a column to a constant fails with an internal-looking error when that column happens to be NULL in every row of the table:

```
Invalid Input Error: BindBuiltinScalarFunction did not return a BoundFunctionExpression
```

The query is valid SQL and returns the expected result on 1.5.6. It also works on 2.0 as soon as a single row has a non-NULL value, and with `SET disabled_optimizers = 'statistics_propagation'`. So the same statement runs fine against production data and fails against a small test fixture or a partition where the column was never filled.

My case: a `products` table with a `version` column (`VARCHAR`, e.g. `'1.2.3'`) that is NULL for products that are not versioned, and a filter that keeps the rows whose major version is not `0`. `split_part` is only how I ran into it; the minimal shape is a `CASE` that folds to NULL over an all-NULL column, compared with a constant (`split_part` is a macro over exactly that shape in 2.0).

Cause, from reading the code: statistics propagation folds `version IS NOT NULL` to `false`, the `CASE` becomes a NULL constant, and `PropagateComparison` rewrites the comparison into `constant_or_null(true, <NULL constant>, '0')` via `ExpressionRewriter::ConstantOrNull` -> `BindBuiltinScalarFunction`. Since dff7d2a1f5 ("replace current varargs with args/kwargs") that bind goes through `FunctionBinder::BindScalarFunction(entry, ...)`, whose `DEFAULT_NULL_HANDLING` shortcut replaces a call with a known-NULL argument by a NULL constant. `BindBuiltinScalarFunction` requires a `BoundFunctionExpression` back and throws. The same throw is reachable from `UNNEST(NULL::STRUCT)` (#26643); any of the planner/optimizer callers of `BindBuiltinScalarFunction` that passes a NULL constant argument hits it.



### To Reproduce


```sql
CREATE TABLE products(version VARCHAR);
INSERT INTO products VALUES (NULL), (NULL), (NULL);

SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE split_part(version, '.', 1) <> '0';
```

Expected (1.5.6):

```
0
```

Actual (`v2.0.0-alpha44738`, also the current `v2.0-cyanoptera` head `c29eca15a`):

```
Invalid Input Error: BindBuiltinScalarFunction did not return a BoundFunctionExpression
```

Minimal shape without `split_part`:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE (CASE WHEN version IS NOT NULL THEN 'a' END) <> '0';
```

```
Invalid Input Error: BindBuiltinScalarFunction did not return a BoundFunctionExpression
```

Variations that work, all on the same 2.0 binary:

```sql
-- disable the optimizer that triggers it
SET disabled_optimizers = 'statistics_propagation';
SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE split_part(version, '.', 1) <> '0';   -- 0

-- one non-NULL row defeats the statistics shortcut
INSERT INTO products VALUES ('1.2.3');
SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE split_part(version, '.', 1) <> '0';   -- 1

-- a different comparison operator takes another code path
SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE split_part(version, '.', 1) IS DISTINCT FROM '0';   -- 3 (before the insert)
```

`=`, `<`, `>` etc. fail the same way as `<>`.


### OS:

Amazon Linux 2023, x86_64 (kernel 6.12)

### DuckDB Version:

v2.0.0-alpha44738 at df47ba32d9, also reproduced on a release build of `v2.0-cyanoptera` at c29eca15a

### DuckDB Client:

CLI

### Hardware:

_No response_

### Full Name:

Dixit Sabharwal

### Affiliation:

AWS Development Center GmbH

- [x] Yes, I have

### Did you include all code required to reproduce the issue?

- [x] Yes, I have

Not applicable - the reproduction does not require a data set

 }

+	             ->HasError());
+	// with a string view column the filters stay above the scan, which also returns the columns they read. The test
+	// factory returns every column and ignores pushed down filters, so each query reads both columns.

+	    "GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL",
+	    "SELECT * FROM %s WHERE flag < 1 AND name IN ('VPG', 'ISUZU', 'SMART', 'LUCID', 'LOTUS') ORDER BY ALL LIMIT 3"};
+	// without unused_columns, a scan of every column has an empty projection list
+	for (auto disabled_optimizers : {"", "unused_columns"}) {
+		REQUIRE(!con.Query(StringUtil::Format("SET disabled_optimizers = '%s'", disabled_optimizers))->HasError());

title: Internal error when a filtered but unselected table-function column feeds a hash join
body:
### What happens?

A query can fail with an internal error when a table function refuses filter pushdown for a filtered column that is not part of the query projection, and the filtered scan is used on the build side of a hash join.

The query fails with:
```SQL
INTERNAL Error: Attempted to access index 2 within vector of size 2
```

The database is then invalidated:
```SQL
FATAL Error: Failed: database has been invalidated because of a previous fatal error
```
The query works on DuckDB 1.5.6, but crashes on newer development builds.

### To Reproduce

```python 
import duckdb
import pyarrow as pa

dim = pa.table({
    "id": pa.array(range(1, 11), pa.int64()),
    "region": pa.array(
        ["a" if i % 2 else "b" for i in range(1, 11)],
        pa.string_view(),
    ),
})

fact = pa.table({
    "id": pa.array(range(1, 1001), pa.int64()),
    "total": pa.array([i * 10 for i in range(1, 1001)], pa.int64()),
})

con = duckdb.connect()
con.register("dim", dim)
con.register("fact", fact)

con.execute("""
    SELECT f.total
    FROM fact f
    JOIN dim d ON f.id = d.id
    WHERE d.region = 'b'
    ORDER BY 1
""").fetchall()
```

Expected result:
```sql
[(20,), (40,), (60,), (80,), (100,)]
```
Actual result:
```sql
InternalException: INTERNAL Error: Attempted to access index 2 within vector of size 2
```
The problem occurs because region is filtered but not selected. The Arrow table function refuses filter pushdown for the `string_view` column, and the fallback filter path exposes an extra column to the hash join.

### OS:

macOS, Apple Silicon (arm64)

### DuckDB Version:

2.0.0.dev2610162032 (source id f8f3f4dcd9); works on 1.5.6

### DuckDB Client:

Python 3.14.4, PyArrow 26.0.0

title: Window sum() over a FLOAT column returns wrong values under memory pressure (silently)
body:
### What happens?

A floating-point `sum()` window aggregate returns wrong values when the window operator runs under memory pressure. With a 4 GB `memory_limit` and 20 threads, `sum(x) OVER (PARTITION BY grp ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)` over 13 M single-row partitions is wrong for 12,999,792 of the 13,000,000 rows: the value returned is not the row's own `x`. With a 40 GB limit the same query is correct for every row.

Only the floating-point sum is affected. A `last_value()` over the same window and an integer `sum()` are correct. It needs a second window function over the same frame (here `last_value(y)`; a `count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` computed in a subquery triggers it too). A query with the `sum()` alone, or with two `sum()`s, does not reproduce it. Disabling the `window_self_join`, `window_rewriter` or `compressed_materialization` optimizers does not help, and neither does casting `x` to `DOUBLE`.

We hit this in a production pipeline (trip chains: the sum of a FLOAT path length over each chain). A one-week run was correct and a one-month run was wrong for 99.99 % of the chains.

### To Reproduce

```python
import tempfile
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute(f"SET threads = 20; SET memory_limit = '4GB'; SET temp_directory = '{tempfile.mkdtemp()}'")
con.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE t AS
    SELECT i AS id, (hash(i) % 1000000)::FLOAT / 10 AS x, (hash(i * 3) % 100000)::DOUBLE AS y
    FROM range(13000000) r(i)""")
# every partition holds exactly one row, so sum(x) over the whole partition must equal x
con.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE w AS
    SELECT id, last_value(y) OVER win AS last_y, sum(x) OVER win AS sum_x
    FROM (SELECT t.*, t.id AS grp FROM t)
    WINDOW win AS (PARTITION BY grp ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)""")
print(con.execute("""
    SELECT count(*) FILTER (abs(w.sum_x - t.x) > 1e-3) AS wrong_sum, count(*) FILTER (w.last_y <> t.y) AS wrong_last
    FROM w JOIN t USING (id)""").fetchall())
```

Output:

| DuckDB | memory_limit | wrong `sum(x)` | wrong `last_value(y)` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.5.5 | 4GB | 12,999,792 | 0 |
| 1.5.6 | 4GB | 12,999,792 | 0 |
| 2.0.0 | 4GB | 12,999,792 | 0 |
| 2.0.1.dev2610211350 | 4GB | 12,999,792 | 0 |
| 2.0.0 | 40GB | 0 | 0 |

Expected: 0 wrong rows at any memory limit (or an out-of-memory error, never silently wrong values).

### OS:

Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64

### DuckDB Version:

1.5.5, 1.5.6, 2.0.0, 2.0.1.dev2610211350

### DuckDB Client:

Python 3.12

### Hardware:

20 vCPUs, 43 GB RAM

Ludovico Lemma

MindEarth

Yes (the data is generated in the script)

title: lpad/rpad ~75% slower in 2.0.0 than in 1.5.5 (ASCII pad character)
body:
### What happens?

`lpad` and `rpad` with a one-byte (ASCII) pad string take about 1.75× as long on v2.0.0 as on v1.5.5. The cost grows with the target length, so it shows mostly on long pads. On one thread, padding 2 million short strings to 200 characters takes 1.15 s on 1.5.5 and 2.03 s on 2.0.0.

| statement (2M rows, threads = 1) | v1.5.5 | v2.0.0 |
|---|---:|---:|
| `lpad(i::VARCHAR, 18, '0')` | 0.138 s | 0.208 s |
| `lpad(i::VARCHAR, 50, '0')` | 0.328 s | 0.548 s |
| `lpad(i::VARCHAR, 200, '0')` | 1.148 s | 2.030 s |
| `rpad(i::VARCHAR, 200, '0')` | 1.165 s | 2.061 s |
| `repeat('0', 200) \|\| i::VARCHAR` (same work, for comparison) | 0.142 s | 0.154 s |

Both 2.0 changes to `extension/core_functions/scalar/string/pad.cpp` touch the per-character loop, and either might cause it:
- #26485 replaced `utf8proc_iterate` with `DecodeCodepoint` in `PadCountChars` and `InsertPadding`.
- #26482 added `CheckPadResultSize`, which calls `PadCountChars` on the pad again for every row.

Separately, `lpad` is about 8× slower than the equivalent `repeat(...) || x` on both versions. It walks the pad one code point at a time. A fast path for a one-byte pad (or for an all-ASCII pad) would avoid that.

We found this through a real workload: an SAP migration job pads 1.66M material numbers with `substr(lpad(x, 200, '0'), 183, 18)`. That expression alone went from 0.96 s to 1.72 s per run.

### To Reproduce

```sql
SET threads = 1;
.timer on
CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP TABLE r AS SELECT lpad(i::VARCHAR, 200, '0') AS t FROM range(2000000) t(i);
CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP TABLE r AS SELECT rpad(i::VARCHAR, 200, '0') AS t FROM range(2000000) t(i);
CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP TABLE r AS SELECT repeat('0', 200) || i::VARCHAR AS t FROM range(2000000) t(i);
```

Run the same script on v1.5.5 and v2.0.0. The `repeat` line is a control: it costs the same on both.

title: Shell sets active_grammar_extensions=['shell'] wholesale, disabling grammar extensions registered by other loaded extensions
body:
### What happens?

Since #26914 the CLI runs `SET active_grammar_extensions=['shell']` on its connection right after opening the database ([`tools/shell/shell.cpp`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/v2.0-cyanoptera/tools/shell/shell.cpp#L1313)). The setting is assigned wholesale: `ActiveGrammarExtensionsSetting::SetLocal` replaces `client_config.active_grammar_extensions` with exactly the given list and compiles a grammar from only those names (`src/main/settings/custom_settings.cpp`, `CompiledGrammar::Create` in `src/main/parser_context.cpp`). A registered `GrammarExtension` whose name is not in the list is not consulted at all.

Consequences in the CLI:

1. An extension that registers a `GrammarExtension` and activates it for new connections from `ExtensionCallback::OnConnectionOpened` is silently disabled, because the shell's `SET` runs after the `Connection` is constructed (connection at line 1290, `SET` at line 1313) and drops the extension's name from the list. Its syntax then fails with a Parser Error in the CLI while parsing fine in every other client (Python, C API, ...), where no `['shell']` assignment happens.
2. Conversely, a user who activates such an extension the documented way, `SET active_grammar_extensions=['my_ext']`, loses the shell grammar: bare expressions / table names as statements stop working. The only working form is to spell out `['shell', 'my_ext']` by hand, which requires knowing that the CLI has an implicit grammar extension named `shell`.

There is no "append" form of the setting (lists are replaced, `RESET` clears), so an extension cannot enable itself without knowing which other grammar extensions the client has turned on, and the client cannot enable its grammar without knowing which extensions are active.

### To Reproduce

Build the CLI with `BUILD_UNITTESTS=1` so the in-tree demo grammar extension `test/extension/loadable_grammar_extension_demo.cpp` (registers a `GrammarExtension` named `pipe_query_syntax`) is built, then:

```
$ build/release/duckdb -unsigned
D SELECT current_setting('active_grammar_extensions') AS before_load;
┌─────────────┐
│ before_load │
├─────────────┤
│ [shell]     │
└─────────────┘
D LOAD 'build/release/test/extension/loadable_grammar_extension_demo.duckdb_extension';
D CREATE TABLE produce(item VARCHAR, sales INTEGER);
D INSERT INTO produce VALUES ('apples', 10), ('bananas', 20);
D FROM produce |> WHERE item != 'bananas';
Parser Error: syntax error at or near "|>"

LINE 1: FROM produce |> WHERE item != 'bananas';
                     ^^
D SET active_grammar_extensions=['shell','pipe_query_syntax'];
D FROM produce |> WHERE item != 'bananas';
┌────────┬───────┐
│  item  │ sales │
├────────┼───────┤
│ apples │ 10    │
└────────┴───────┘
D 1 + 1;
┌─────────┐
│ (1 + 1) │
├─────────┤
│ 2       │
└─────────┘
D SET active_grammar_extensions=['pipe_query_syntax'];
D FROM produce |> WHERE item != 'bananas';
┌────────┬───────┐
│  item  │ sales │
├────────┼───────┤
│ apples │ 10    │
└────────┴───────┘
D 1 + 1;
Parser Error: syntax error at or near "1"

LINE 1: 1 + 1;
        ^
```

The demo extension does not activate itself, so step 1 above is shown by code pointers: an extension that calls `GrammarExtension::Register(db, ...)` in `Load` and `SET active_grammar_extensions=['my_ext']` (or sets `ClientConfig::active_grammar_extensions`) in `OnConnectionOpened` ends up with `['shell']` on the CLI connection, since `shell.cpp` line 1313 runs after the connection has been opened. `test/extension/test_loadable_grammar_extension.test` passes in the sqllogictest runner because there the connection has no `shell` entry to begin with.

Possible fixes:

- the shell adds its own name to the current list instead of replacing it (read `current_setting('active_grammar_extensions')`, append `shell`), and does so in a way that also survives a later `SET` by an extension or user; or
- the setting gets a merge/append form (or an `ADD`/`REMOVE` variant) so clients and extensions can enable their grammar without knowing about each other; or
- the shell grammar is enabled through a dedicated boolean (for example `shell_expression_statements`) rather than through the shared `active_grammar_extensions` list, so the list keeps meaning "extensions the user asked for".

### OS:

Linux (aarch64)

### DuckDB Version:

v2.0.0-dev build of `v2.0-cyanoptera` containing d4355d01c59 (introduced by #26914, merged 2026-10-13)

CLI

title: Performance regression from 1.5.6 to 2.0: selective STRUCT-field LATERAL query processes all recursive partitions
body:
### What happens?

A selective correlated LATERAL query involving a computed STRUCT field processes
all recursive partitions in DuckDB 2.0, whereas DuckDB 1.5.6 processes only the
matching partition.

Both versions return the correct result, 5. With 1000 input rows, the recursive
CTE emits 3 rows on 1.5.6 and 3000 rows on 2.0. This is a regression in recursive
work; no wall-clock slowdown factor is claimed.

### To Reproduce

Run the following SQL in a fresh database using the DuckDB CLI. It generates
its own data and writes a profile to /tmp. The final query supports the JSON
profiling field names used by both tested versions.

```sql
CREATE TABLE person AS SELECT i AS id FROM range(1000) t(i);
CREATE VIEW nodes AS SELECT id, struct_pack(k := id) AS node FROM person;
PRAGMA enable_profiling='json';
SET profiling_output='/tmp/duckdb-struct-regression.json';
SELECT max(q.x)
FROM nodes o, LATERAL (
 SELECT r.x FROM nodes i, LATERAL (
  WITH RECURSIVE walk(x) AS (
   SELECT i.node.k
   UNION ALL SELECT x+1 FROM walk WHERE x < i.node.k+2
  ) SELECT x FROM walk
 ) r
 WHERE i.node.k = o.node.k
) q WHERE o.id=3;
PRAGMA disable_profiling;
SELECT sum(coalesce(
 (value->>'intermediate_rows')::BIGINT,
 (value->>'operator_cardinality')::BIGINT
)) AS recursive_rows
FROM read_text('/tmp/duckdb-struct-regression.json'), json_tree(content)
WHERE coalesce(value->>'type', value->>'operator_type') = 'RECURSIVE_CTE';
```

Output on DuckDB 1.5.6:

```text
max(q.x): 5
recursive_rows: 3
```

Output on DuckDB 2.0:

```text
max(q.x): 5
recursive_rows: 3000
```

Expected: restrict recursive execution to the matching partition, as observed
on 1.5.6. Replacing range(1000) with range(4) still reproduces the difference:
3 recursive rows on 1.5.6 versus 12 on 2.0.

Default optimizer settings were used. The 2.0 CLI was rebuilt from the tested
checkout. The precise optimizer cause has not been established.

### OS:

macOS 27.0.1, arm64

### DuckDB Version:

Affected: v2.0.0-dev87731 (source ID c65ca930b9, branch v2.0-cyanoptera).
Baseline: v1.5.6 (source ID 069cc9f9b5).

### DuckDB Client:

DuckDB CLI

### Hardware:

Apple M1 Max, 32 GiB RAM

### Full Name:

wangqiang

### Affiliation:

Independent

- [x] Yes, I have

### Did you include all code required to reproduce the issue?

- [x] Yes, I have

### Did you include all relevant data sets for reproducing the issue?

Yes — all data is generated by the SQL above.

+        ) SELECT y FROM walk2
+    ) r WHERE j.id = o.id
+) b WHERE o.id=5;
+----
+7	8
+
+statement ok
+PRAGMA disable_profiling;
+
+query I
+SELECT recursive_rows();
+----
+7
+
+# Semi joins restrict the partitions of correlated EXISTS subqueries
+
+statement ok
+PRAGMA enable_profiling='json';
+
+query I
+SELECT count(*) FROM person o WHERE o.id=3 AND EXISTS (
+    SELECT 1 FROM person i, LATERAL (
+        WITH RECURSIVE walk(x) AS (
+            SELECT i.id UNION ALL SELECT x+1 FROM walk WHERE x < i.id+2
+        ) SELECT x FROM walk
+    ) r WHERE i.id = o.id AND r.x > 4
+);
+----
+1
+
+statement ok
+PRAGMA disable_profiling;
+
+query I
+SELECT recursive_rows();
+----
+3
+
+# Prepared statement parameters survive copying the key domain
+
+statement ok
+PREPARE walk_sel AS SELECT max(q.x)
+FROM person o, LATERAL (
+    SELECT r.x FROM person i, LATERAL (
+        WITH RECURSIVE walk(x) AS (
+            SELECT i.id UNION ALL SELECT x+1 FROM walk WHERE x < i.id+2
+        ) SELECT x FROM walk
+    ) r
+    WHERE i.id = o.id
+) q WHERE o.id=$1;
+
+statement ok
+PRAGMA enable_profiling='json';
+
+query I
+EXECUTE walk_sel(3);
+----
+5
+
+statement ok
+PRAGMA disable_profiling;
+
+query I
+SELECT recursive_rows();
+----
+3
+
 # Disabling the coordinating pass must retain all recursive partitions.
 statement ok
 SET disabled_optimizers='cte_filter_pusher';

title: Unicode whitespace shifts parser error byte offsets
body:
### What happens?

Normalizing Unicode whitespace shortens the SQL string before parsing. As a result, parser error positions after that whitespace no longer point to the correct UTF-8 byte in the submitted SQL. Clients using the reported position to highlight an error can highlight the wrong location.

### To Reproduce

Run this in the DuckDB CLI. `chr(160)` creates a non-breaking space, and `chr(8195)` creates an em space:

```sql
SELECT
    (json_serialize_sql('SELECT' || chr(160) || ')')->>'position')::INTEGER AS nbsp_position,
    (json_serialize_sql('SELECT' || chr(8195) || ')')->>'position')::INTEGER AS em_space_position;
```

Actual result:

```text
nbsp_position  em_space_position
7              7
```

Expected result:

```text
nbsp_position  em_space_position
8              9
```

The error is the closing `)`. `SELECT` occupies six bytes; the non-breaking space occupies two bytes and the em space occupies three. The expected positions are therefore zero-based UTF-8 byte offsets 8 and 9.

A fix is proposed in #27835, targeting `main`. Please have the DuckDB team backport the merged fix to the v2.0 release branch (`v2.0-cyanoptera`).

### OS:

Amazon Linux 2023, aarch64.

### DuckDB Version:

`main` at `1641475ef1db08ec063631ff6a8f08d9d6736ae7`.

### DuckDB Client:

DuckDB CLI.

title: SQL formatter inserts whitespace into parameters and treats keyword parameter names as clauses
body:
### What happens?

`duckdb_format_sql` formats the `$` prefix and the following parameter name separately. This inserts whitespace inside parameters such as `$customer` and `$1`. If the name is a keyword, such as `$select`, the formatter also treats it as a SQL keyword or clause instead of part of the parameter.

This affects the core `FormatSQL` implementation used by the formatter. Formatting should preserve parameter spelling while applying the selected keyword case to SQL keywords.

### To Reproduce

```sql
LOAD autocomplete;
SELECT duckdb_format_sql('select $customer, $1');
SELECT duckdb_format_sql('select $select');
SELECT duckdb_format_sql('SELECT $YEAR', MAP {'keyword_case': 'lower'});
```

Expected formatted values:

```sql
SELECT $customer, $1
```

```sql
SELECT $select
```

```sql
select $YEAR
```

Actual formatted values on the unpatched build, in the same order:

```sql
SELECT $ customer, $ 1
```

```sql
SELECT $
SELECT
```

```sql
select $ year
```

A fix is proposed in #27834, targeting `main`. Please have the DuckDB team backport the merged fix to the v2.0 release branch (`v2.0-cyanoptera`).

### OS:

Amazon Linux 2023, aarch64.

### DuckDB Version:

`main` at `1641475ef1db08ec063631ff6a8f08d9d6736ae7`.

### DuckDB Client:

DuckDB CLI.

+# A parameter at the beginning of a multiline clause must remain a single token.

+    $select

+----

+
+endloop
+
+endloop

title: List-comprehension rewrite drops casts and returns incorrect results
body:
### What happens?

The list-comprehension expression rewrite drops value-changing casts from a supported nested `list_transform`/`list_filter` expression. The query below returns `[2]` with the optimizer enabled and `[1]` with it disabled. The correct result is `[1]`: `2::BOOLEAN::INTEGER` is `1`, and `list_transform` must apply its complete lambda expression to each element.

This can also discard a filter's intermediate casts, turn `TRY_CAST` into a throwing cast, or produce an internal physical-vector-type error when a result cast changes the physical type.

### To Reproduce

```sql
SELECT list_transform(
    list_filter(list_transform(l, lambda x: struct_pack(filter := true, result := x)), lambda s: s.filter),
    lambda s: s.result::BOOLEAN::INTEGER
) FROM (VALUES ([2])) t(l);

PRAGMA disable_optimizer;

SELECT list_transform(
    list_filter(list_transform(l, lambda x: struct_pack(filter := true, result := x)), lambda s: s.filter),
    lambda s: s.result::BOOLEAN::INTEGER
) FROM (VALUES ([2])) t(l);
```

Actual outputs, in order:

```text
[2]
[1]
```

Expected: `[1]` for both queries. Disabling only `expression_rewriter` also restores the correct result. [The documented `list_transform` contract](https://duckdb.org/docs/current/sql/functions/lambda) is to apply the lambda to every input element and use its return type.

### Root cause

In `src/optimizer/rule/list_comprehension_rewrite.cpp`, `MatchesStructFieldProjection` and `MatchListComprehensionRewrite` use `UnwrapCasts` to recognize the parser's `filter`/`result` struct pattern. `BuildListComprehensionRewrite` then copies the original `struct_pack` children into the new filter/transform lambdas, without recreating the casts that were unwrapped. These casts are not generally identity operations, even when the final type equals the original type.

A focused local regression fails on the untouched revision below with `[2] <> [1]`. Restricting recognition to exact projections/packing, while retaining the one ordinary Boolean filter cast that the rewrite already recreates, restores the result. Boundary coverage includes filter/result/struct casts, `TRY_CAST`, NULL and empty lists, 6145 rows, and prepared execution, with the optimizer enabled and disabled.

### Environment

- OS: macOS 15.7.3, arm64.
- DuckDB version: `v2.1.0-dev84887`, untouched upstream `main` at `e829ad15292587f35a6725026684d361831ff19c`.
- Client: native DuckDB CLI and SQLLogicTest, built using `CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL=6 GEN=ninja make reldebug`.
- No external dataset or extension is needed.

### Identity disclosure

- Full name: Henry Su.
- Affiliation: GitHub profile bio states “cs & math @ tamu”.

The investigation and local patch were prepared with Codex. Public issues, PRs, discussions, commits, tests and release notes were searched using both the SQL symptoms and matcher symbols; no blocking overlap was found. Original rewrite PR #21025 is related, but does not report this cast-loss behavior. Private internal tracker contents were not accessible.
fix_test_text:
--- test/sql/optimizer/expression/list_comprehension_casts.test
@@ -0,0 +1,102 @@
+# name: test/sql/optimizer/expression/list_comprehension_casts.test
+# description: Preserve casts in nested list lambda rewrites
+# group: [expression]
+
+foreach optimizer enable disable
+
+statement ok
+PRAGMA {optimizer}_optimizer;
+
+# A lossy round trip must not be replaced with the original value.
+query I
+SELECT list_transform(
+	list_filter(list_transform(l, lambda x: struct_pack(filter := true, result := x)), lambda s: s.filter),
+	lambda s: s.result::BOOLEAN::INTEGER
+) FROM (VALUES ([2])) t(l);
+----
+[1]
+
+# Changing the result's physical type must also preserve the cast.
+query I
+SELECT list_transform(
+	list_filter(list_transform(l, lambda x: struct_pack(filter := true, result := x)), lambda s: s.filter),
+	lambda s: s.result::VARCHAR
+) FROM (VALUES ([2])) t(l);
+----
+[2]
+
+# A filter's intermediate cast can change which elements qualify.
+query I
+SELECT list_transform(
+	list_filter(list_transform(l, lambda x: struct_pack(filter := x, result := x)),
+	            lambda s: s.filter::DECIMAL(1,0)::BOOLEAN),
+	lambda s: s.result
+) FROM (VALUES ([0.1,0.9])) t(l);
+----
+[0.9]
+
+# TRY_CAST rejects an unconvertible filter value without throwing.
+query I
+SELECT list_transform(
+	list_filter(list_transform(l, lambda x: struct_pack(filter := x, result := x)),
+	            lambda s: TRY_CAST(s.filter AS BOOLEAN)),
+	lambda s: s.result
+) FROM (VALUES (['true','bad'])) t(l);
+----
+[true]
+
+# Casts around the packed struct cannot be discarded either.
+query I
+SELECT list_transform(
+	list_filter(list_transform(l, lambda x: struct_pack(filter := true, result := x)
+	            ::STRUCT(filter BOOLEAN,result BOOLEAN)::STRUCT(filter BOOLEAN,result INTEGER)), lambda s: s.filter),
+	lambda s: s.result
+) FROM (VALUES ([2])) t(l);
+----
+[1]
+
+# The struct used by a field projection may itself have been converted.
+query I
+SELECT list_transform(
+	list_filter(list_transform(l, lambda x: struct_pack(filter := true, result := x)), lambda s: s.filter),
+	lambda s: (s::STRUCT(filter BOOLEAN,result BOOLEAN)::STRUCT(filter BOOLEAN,result INTEGER)).result
+) FROM (VALUES ([2])) t(l);
+----
+[1]
+
+query I
+SELECT list_transform(
+	list_filter(list_transform(l, lambda x: struct_pack(filter := true, result := x)), lambda s: s.filter),
+	lambda s: s.result::BOOLEAN::INTEGER
+) FROM (VALUES (1, [0,2,NULL,-3]), (2, []), (3, NULL)) t(id,l) ORDER BY id;
+----
+[0, 1, NULL, 1]
+[]
+NULL
+
+# Exercise more than one vector with a nonconstant list column.
+query I
+SELECT count(*) FROM (
+	SELECT list_transform(
+		list_filter(list_transform([i + 2], lambda x: struct_pack(filter := true, result := x)), lambda s: s.filter),
+		lambda s: s.result::BOOLEAN::BIGINT
+	) AS l FROM range(6145) t(i)
+) t WHERE l = [1];
+----
+6145
+
+statement ok
+PREPARE list_cast AS SELECT list_transform(
+	list_filter(list_transform(l, lambda x: struct_pack(filter := true, result := x)), lambda s: s.filter),
+	lambda s: s.result::BOOLEAN::INTEGER
+) FROM (VALUES ($1)) t(l);
+
+query I
+EXECUTE list_cast([2]);
+----
+[1]
+
+statement ok
+DEALLOCATE list_cast;
+
+endloop

title: INSERT with ON CONFLICT / OR IGNORE / OR REPLACE skips column-list checks: wrong rows inserted or INTERNAL Error
body:
### What happens?

`INSERT INTO t (column list) ...` rejects an invalid column list (unknown column, too many values, generated column). With `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING / DO UPDATE` or `INSERT OR IGNORE`, the same statements succeed and insert wrong rows. This happens with a SELECT source; for a generated column it also happens with VALUES. With `INSERT OR REPLACE`, an unknown column gives an INTERNAL Error.

### To Reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE w (i INT UNIQUE, j INT, g AS (j * 2));

INSERT INTO w (zz) SELECT 1 ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
INSERT INTO w (r) SELECT 1 ON CONFLICT (i) DO UPDATE SET j = 0;
INSERT OR IGNORE INTO w (i) SELECT 5, 6;
INSERT INTO w (g) VALUES (4) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

SELECT * FROM w;

INSERT OR REPLACE INTO w (zz) SELECT 1;
-- INTERNAL Error: Column with name "zz" does not exist
```

### OS:

Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64

### DuckDB Version:

v1.4.5, v1.5.5, v2.0.0-alpha43385

### DuckDB Client:

Python

title: Wrong result: in_clause rewrite duplicates volatile LHS, so nextval() IN (...) is evaluated more than once
body:
### What happens?

`InClauseRewriter::VisitReplace` rewrites a short `IN` list into a disjunction of equalities and copies the
left-hand side expression for every list element without checking whether it is volatile
(`src/optimizer/in_clause_rewriter.cpp:96-103`).

For `X IN (1, 2)` this yields `(X = 1) OR (X = 2)`, where `X` is evaluated **twice**. With `nextval()` (or
`random()`, `uuid()`, etc.) each evaluation returns a different value, so the result differs from evaluating
`X` once.

### To Reproduce


```sql
CREATE SEQUENCE seq START 2;

-- Default (in_clause enabled)
SELECT nextval('seq') IN (1, 2);
-- actual: false
-- (first nextval() -> 2, 2 = 1 is false; second nextval() -> 3, 3 = 2 is false)

-- Correct behavior
SET disabled_optimizers = 'in_clause';
CREATE SEQUENCE seq2 START 2;
SELECT nextval('seq2') IN (1, 2);
-- actual: true  (evaluated once: 2 IN (1, 2))
```

The same shape with `random()`:
```sql
SET seed = 0;
SELECT (random() * 2)::INT IN (0, 1);  -- may return false even though the value is 0 or 1
```

### Expected vs Actual

- Expected: `true` (`nextval` evaluated exactly once per row; SQL standard requires the LHS to be evaluated once).
- Actual with `in_clause`: `false`.

### Root cause

`in_clause_rewriter.cpp:96-103` builds one comparison per list element using
`expr.GetChildrenMutable()[0]->Copy()` and never checks `IsVolatile()`. The rewrite is only equivalence-preserving
for deterministic LHS expressions.

### Suggested fix

Skip the rewrite (leave the `COMPARE_IN` expression intact) when `expr.GetChildrenMutable()[0]->IsVolatile()`,
mirroring the existing volatility guards used elsewhere in the optimizer. Alternatively, rewrite to
`(SELECT x FROM (VALUES (X)) t(x)) ...` so the LHS is materialized once, but a volatility bail-out is simpler and
matches DuckDB's usual conservative policy.

### OS:

macOS 15 (arm64)

### DuckDB Version:

2.0.0 (d54cbbe)

### DuckDB Client:

Python

### Hardware:

Apple Silicon (M-series)

### Full Name:

Cheng Wang

### Affiliation:

Independent Researcher

### Did you include all relevant configuration (e.g., CPU architecture, Linux distribution) to reproduce the issue?

- [x] Yes, I have

### Did you include all code required to reproduce the issue?

- [x] Yes, I have

### Did you include all relevant data sets for reproducing the issue?

No - Other reason (please specify in the issue body)

title: TPC-DS Q64 regression on main: join_order optimizer introduces MARK join causing OOM at SF1000
body:
## Summary

TPC-DS Q64 completes in ~40s on v1.5.1 but gets OOM-killed on main at SF1000. The join_order optimizer on main introduces a MARK join pattern for the `cs_ui` CTE's HAVING clause that doesn't exist on v1.5.1. This creates a plan with NESTED_LOOP execution that causes unbounded memory growth.

## Reproducing

```sql
-- TPC-DS Q64 at SF1000 (or SF100 for smaller repro)
-- Standard TPC-DS query, no modifications
INSTALL tpcds; LOAD tpcds;
SELECT query FROM tpcds_queries() WHERE query_nr=64;
```

**Settings**: `SET memory_limit='220GB'; SET threads=48;`

| Version | Time | Spill | Result |
|---------|------|-------|--------|
| v1.5.1 | 36-53s | 0-82GB | OK |
| main (538d289) | 132s | 96GB | OOM killed (SIGKILL) |

The issue reproduces consistently across multiple runs.

## Root cause

Q64 defines a `cs_ui` CTE with a HAVING clause:

```sql
WITH cs_ui AS (
    SELECT cs_item_sk, sum(cs_ext_list_price) AS sale,
           sum(cr_refunded_cash+cr_reversed_charge+cr_store_credit) AS refund
    FROM catalog_sales, catalog_returns
    WHERE cs_item_sk = cr_item_sk AND cs_order_number = cr_order_number
    GROUP BY cs_item_sk
    HAVING sum(cs_ext_list_price) > 2*sum(cr_refunded_cash+cr_reversed_charge+cr_store_credit)
)
```

This CTE feeds into `cross_sales`, an 18-table join referenced twice with different year filters (`cs1.syear = 1999`, `cs2.syear = 2000`).

Comparing EXPLAIN output between v1.5.1 and main:

| | v1.5.1 | main |
|---|---|---|
| HASH_JOIN | 17 | 17 |
| NESTED_LOOP | **0** | **1** |
| MARK join | **0** | **1** |
| HASH_GROUP_BY | 1 | 2 |

The join_order optimizer on main converts the HAVING-filtered CTE join into a MARK semi-join pattern, which executes as a NESTED_LOOP. At SF1000, this causes OOM.

## Bisecting the optimizer

I tested disabling individual optimizers on main via `SET disabled_optimizers`:

| Disabled optimizer | NESTED_LOOP? | MARK? | SF1000 result |
|---|---|---|---|
| *(none)* | Yes | 1 | OOM killed |
| `join_order` | **No** | **0** | TIMEOUT (CPU, no spill) |
| `deliminator` | Yes | 1 | OOM killed |
| `common_subplan` | Yes | 1 | TIMEOUT (372GB spill) |
| `build_side_probe_side` | Yes | 1 | TIMEOUT (0 spill) |
| `filter_pushdown` | No | 1 | N/A (broken plan) |

Only disabling `join_order` removes the MARK+NESTED_LOOP pattern, but then Q64 has no join optimization at all and times out on CPU.

## Expected behavior

The join_order optimizer should produce a plan using only HASH_JOINs for Q64, like v1.5.1 does. The HAVING clause should remain a simple filter on the GROUP BY output, not be converted to a MARK semi-join.

## Environment

- DuckDB main at commit 538d289fea
- v1.5.1 used as baseline
- TPC-DS SF1000, sorted Parquet
- Linux, 256GB RAM

title: Regression on main: `INSERT INTO <attached postgres/mysql table> (a) …` writes NULL into the omitted columns instead of letting the server apply its DEFAULT (`LogicalInsert::column_index_map` is no longer filled)
body:
### What happens?


On main, an `INSERT` with a column list (or `BY NAME`) into a PostgreSQL or MySQL table attached through the
postgres/mysql extensions stores **NULL** in every omitted column. The server's `DEFAULT` (`'new'`, `now()`, `1`,
…) is not applied. The INSERT succeeds with no warning. If the omitted column is `NOT NULL` with a default
(e.g. `id serial PRIMARY KEY`), every such INSERT fails instead, with `null value in column "id" … violates not-null
constraint`.

1.5.6 with the released extensions applies the defaults correctly. The sqlite extension is not affected, because it
binds SQLite's default expressions on the DuckDB side.

Cause: both extensions decide which columns to send from `LogicalInsert::column_index_map`. An empty map means "the
statement supplies all columns" (duckdb-postgres `src/storage/postgres_insert.cpp:80`, duckdb-mysql
`src/storage/mysql_insert.cpp:60`). In other words, if the map is non-empty they send only the listed columns, and
the server fills in its defaults. Since #23033 ("Resolve `DEFAULT`s for INSERT/UPDATE/MERGE_INTO at bind-time rather
than plan-time", merged 2026-06-14), `Binder::Bind(InsertStatement&)` builds a *local* map
(`src/planner/binder/statement/bind_insert.cpp:660`, passed to `BindInsertColumnList` and `ResolveInputProjection`).
`ResolveInputProjection` uses it to push `insert.bound_defaults[…]` for the omitted columns, but the map is never
stored in `insert->column_index_map`, although the member still exists (`logical_insert.hpp:59`). For a remote table
DuckDB does not know the server-side default, so those bound defaults are NULL constants. The extension then sees an
empty map and sends all columns, including the NULLs.

The `DuckDB` commit pinned by duckdb-postgres main already contains the change, so the extensions' CI build is
affected too. Related: duckdb/duckdb-postgres#487 (`MERGE INTO` sends NULL for omitted columns, on 1.5.2; it states
that plain INSERT works there).

Possible fixes: keep filling `LogicalInsert::column_index_map` (as 1.5 did), or give catalogs a way to say "use the
remote default" for omitted columns.


### To Reproduce


PostgreSQL:

```sql
-- in psql
CREATE TABLE dk119_orders(order_no int, status text DEFAULT 'new', created timestamptz DEFAULT now(), qty int DEFAULT 1);
INSERT INTO dk119_orders(order_no) VALUES (0);
```

```sql
-- in DuckDB
ATTACH 'host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 user=postgres dbname=postgres' AS p (TYPE postgres);
INSERT INTO p.dk119_orders(order_no) VALUES (1);
INSERT INTO p.dk119_orders BY NAME SELECT 2 AS order_no;
INSERT INTO p.dk119_orders(order_no, status) VALUES (3, DEFAULT);
```

```
postgres=# SELECT order_no, status, created IS NOT NULL AS has_created, qty FROM dk119_orders ORDER BY order_no;
 order_no | status | has_created | qty
----------+--------+-------------+-----
        0 | new    | t           |   1        <-- inserted by psql
        1 |        | f           |            <-- main: NULL, NULL, NULL
        2 |        | f           |
        3 |        | f           |
```

With 1.5.6 and its released `postgres_scanner`, rows 1 and 2 get `new | t | 1`.

MySQL (same with `ATTACH '…' AS m (TYPE mysql)`):

```sql
-- in mysql
CREATE TABLE dk119_orders(order_no int, status varchar(10) DEFAULT 'new', qty int DEFAULT 1, created datetime DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP);
INSERT INTO dk119_orders(order_no) VALUES (0);
-- in DuckDB
INSERT INTO m.dk119_orders(order_no) VALUES (1);
```

```
order_no  status  qty   has_created
0         new     1     1
1         NULL    NULL  0              <-- 1.5.6: new, 1, 1
```

Expected: the omitted columns get the server defaults, as in 1.5.6.


### OS:

Ubuntu 22.04.2 LTS, x86_64

### DuckDB Version:

v2.1.0-dev89158 (main 1b4c3e54ba) with duckdb-postgres main c0f5a3c and duckdb-mysql main e130b41, built from source (two one-line `unique_ptr` casts patched in the extensions so they compile against main); 1.5.6 is correct

title: INTERNAL Error "GetPartitioningSpaceRequirement: tuple width should not be 0" for a hash join whose probe side has no columns
body:
### What happens?

With `disabled_optimizers='unused_columns'`, the query below plans a SEMI hash join whose probe side is an
`UNGROUPED_AGGREGATE` with no aggregates, so the probe side has zero columns. During finalize of the hash join
build, `PhysicalHashJoin::PrepareFinalize` sizes the probe-side spill. It computes a row width of 0 for the probe
types and throws an InternalException. The database instance is then invalidated, and every later statement
fails with FATAL until restart.

Plan (`EXPLAIN`, trunk 1b4c3e54ba):

```
PROJECTION  Projections: 0
  HASH_JOIN  Join Type: SEMI; Conditions: 0 = #0
    UNGROUPED_AGGREGATE
      SEQ_SCAN t1
    PROJECTION  Projections: 0
      SEQ_SCAN t1
```

## SQL

```sql
CREATE TABLE t1(c0 INTEGER);
SET disabled_optimizers='unused_columns';
SELECT 0 FROM t1 HAVING 0 IN (SELECT 0 FROM t1);
SELECT 42 AS still_alive;
```

title: SET with an unquoted qualified value keeps only its last name part (regression since v1.5)
body:
### What happens?

In the 2.0 development line, an unquoted qualified name used as a `SET` value is reduced
to its last part: 

For example

`SET VARIABLE v = a.b.c` stores `c`

 and

`SET default_null_order = a.nulls_last` is accepted as `NULLS_LAST` instead of being rejected.

In v1.5.6 the whole value is kept (`a.b.c`), and settings validate it

The previous transformer kept qualified names whole via `expr->ToString()`

```
SET VARIABLE v = a.b.c;
```

yields `c`.

```
SET default_null_order = this_doesnt_exist.nulls_last;
SELECT current_setting('default_null_order') AS null_order;
```

yields `nulls_last`.

 On v1.5.6,

the latter yields 

```
Parser Error: Unrecognized parameter for option NULL_ORDER "a.nulls_last", expected either NULLS FIRST, NULLS LAST, SQLite, MySQL or Postgres
```

title: VARCHAR → DECIMAL cast ~150x slower for width > 18 than width ≤ 18 on Linux
body:
### What happens?

Casting VARCHAR to a DECIMAL that's stored as HUGEINT (width 19–38) is much slower than casting the same strings to a DECIMAL stored as INT64 (width ≤ 18). On Linux the gap is roughly 150x; on macOS, on the same machine, it's roughly 25x.

Parsing into `DECIMAL(18, 10)` and widening to `DECIMAL(28, 10)` gives the same result whenever the value fits in `DECIMAL(18, 10)` (≤8 integer digits here), and it's as fast as the narrow cast on both OSes.

Timings for 10M strings, 4 threads, DuckDB 1.5.6, same Apple M4 Pro (the Linux runs are in an arm64 Docker container):

| Cast | macOS arm64 | Linux arm64 |
|---|---|---|
| VARCHAR → DECIMAL(18, 10) | 0.06s | 0.07s |
| VARCHAR → DECIMAL(28, 10) | 1.59s | 10.93s |
| VARCHAR → DECIMAL(38, 10) | 1.55s | 10.93s |
| VARCHAR → DECIMAL(18, 10) → DECIMAL(28, 10) | 0.07s | 0.07s |

`2.0.0.dev2610011535` behaves the same as 1.5.6 (3.5s vs 0.05s on the same real-data column, Linux arm64).

In our pipeline on Linux x86_64 (AMD, Modal), the same pattern shows on real data in a different query: 7.1s vs 0.11s for 7.8M values. There, these casts accounted for most of the query time: a 19M-row transform went from 78s to 32s after switching to the narrow-then-widen cast.

**Expected:** since the narrow-then-widen cast is exact and fast when the value fits in 18 digits, the direct cast should be close to that speed. Two things look worth checking:
1. the HUGEINT string-parse path in general (~25x slower than INT64 even on macOS);
2. why it's a further ~7x slower on Linux builds. Possibly the 128-bit multiply / overflow-check codegen differs between toolchains, but I haven't verified that.

### To Reproduce

```python
import duckdb, platform, time

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute("set threads = 4")
# 10M decimal strings like '12345.6789012345' (5 integer + 10 fractional digits)
con.execute("""
create table t as
select printf('%d.%010d', (random() * 100000)::bigint, (random() * 10000000000)::bigint) as s
from range(10000000)
""")
print(f"duckdb {duckdb.__version__} | {platform.system()} {platform.machine()}")
for target in ["decimal(18, 10)", "decimal(28, 10)", "decimal(38, 10)"]:
    t = time.perf_counter()
    con.execute(f"select sum(cast(s as {target})) from t").fetchone()
    print(f"  varchar -> {target}: {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")
t = time.perf_counter()
con.execute("select sum(cast(cast(s as decimal(18, 10)) as decimal(28, 10))) from t").fetchone()
print(f"  varchar -> decimal(18, 10) -> decimal(28, 10): {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")
```

Run it natively on macOS, then in `docker run --platform linux/arm64 python:3.13-slim` (with `pip install duckdb==1.5.6`) on the same machine.

title: After ALTER TABLE on a foreign-key child table, the parent table can be renamed, and CHECKPOINT then never returns
body:
### What happens?

While table `c` has a foreign key to `p`, `ALTER TABLE p RENAME TO p2` is refused. After `ALTER TABLE c ADD COLUMN x INT`, the same rename succeeds. Afterwards, every INSERT into `c` fails, and on a file database `CHECKPOINT` does not return.

### To Reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE p (a INT PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE c (k INT, FOREIGN KEY (k) REFERENCES p (a));
ALTER TABLE p RENAME TO p2;
-- Dependency Error: Cannot alter entry "p" because there are entries that depend on it.
ALTER TABLE c ADD COLUMN x INT;
```

title: Join order optimizer drops a filter that references no column (`WHERE NULL`, `WHERE random() > 2`) when filter_pushdown is disabled
body:
### What happens?

If a filter predicate references no column of any relation (a constant like `WHERE NULL`, or something volatile
like `WHERE random() > 2`) and ends up between reorderable joins, the join order optimizer removes it from the plan.
A simple way to get there: disable `filter_pushdown`. A query with two uncorrelated scalar subqueries in the SELECT
list then returns its rows unfiltered. `WHERE NULL` returns a row, and `WHERE random() > 2` returns every row.

## To Reproduce

  ```sql
  CREATE TABLE t0(c0 INTEGER);
  INSERT INTO t0 VALUES (1);
  SET disabled_optimizers='filter_pushdown';
  SELECT (SELECT 1) AS a0, (SELECT 2) AS a1 FROM t0 WHERE NULL;
  ```

  Expected: 0 rows. `WHERE NULL` keeps no rows, and with default settings DuckDB returns 0 rows.

  Actual (v2.1.0-dev89158, 1b4c3e54ba, and v1.5.6):

  ```
  ┌───────┬───────┐
  │  a0   │  a1   │
  ├───────┼───────┤
  │     1 │     2 │
  └───────┴───────┘
  ```


### To Reproduce

  ```sql
  CREATE TABLE t0(c0 INTEGER);
  INSERT INTO t0 VALUES (1);
  SET disabled_optimizers='filter_pushdown';
  SELECT (SELECT 1) AS a0, (SELECT 2) AS a1 FROM t0 WHERE NULL;
  ```

title: `EXPORT DATABASE … (FORMAT CSV)` in upper case still loses empty strings on `IMPORT DATABASE` (follow-up to #25501 / #26582)
body:
### What happens?


#26582 fixed #25501: `EXPORT DATABASE 'exp' (FORMAT csv)` now writes `allow_quoted_nulls false` (plus
`quote`/`delimiter`/`header`) into `load.sql`, so empty strings come back as empty strings. The fix only works for
the **lower-case** spelling. With `(FORMAT CSV)`, the spelling used in most examples, `load.sql` contains just
`(FORMAT 'CSV')`. `IMPORT DATABASE` then turns every `''` of `VARCHAR`, `BLOB` and `ENUM` columns into NULL. A
`NOT NULL` column holding `''` makes the import fail.

The CSV data files are the same for both spellings. Only the generated `load.sql` differs.

Cause: the export keeps the format name as typed, and two places compare it case-sensitively:
- `src/execution/operator/persistent/physical_export.cpp:69`, `if (info.format == "csv")`. This guards the
  `force_not_null` list and the `allow_quoted_nulls false` option from #26582.
- `src/planner/binder/statement/bind_export.cpp:288`, `if (format == "csv")`. This adds the default `header`,
  `delimiter` and `quote` options.

The `COPY` binder lower-cases its own copy of the format, but the export's `CopyInfo` is not lower-cased.
Lower-casing the format once in the export binder (or comparing case-insensitively) fixes both.


### To Reproduce


```bash
duckdb src.db "CREATE TYPE mood AS ENUM ('', 'ok');
               CREATE TABLE t(id INT, v VARCHAR, b BLOB, e mood);
               INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, '', ''::BLOB, ''), (2, NULL, NULL, NULL), (3, 'x', 'x'::BLOB, 'ok');
               EXPORT DATABASE 'exp' (FORMAT CSV);"
grep COPY exp/load.sql
duckdb dst.db -csv "IMPORT DATABASE 'exp';
                    SELECT id, v IS NULL AS v_null, b IS NULL AS b_null, e IS NULL AS e_null FROM t ORDER BY id;"
```

Actual with `(FORMAT CSV)`:

```
COPY t FROM 'exp/t.csv' (FORMAT 'CSV');
id,v_null,b_null,e_null
1,true,true,true         <-- were '', ''::BLOB, ''
2,true,true,true
3,false,false,false
```

With `(FORMAT csv)` (correct):

```
COPY t FROM 'exp/t.csv' (FORMAT 'csv', allow_quoted_nulls false, quote '"', delimiter ',', header 1);
id,v_null,b_null,e_null
1,false,false,false
2,true,true,true
3,false,false,false
```

With a `NOT NULL` column that holds `''`, `(FORMAT CSV)` gives:

```
IMPORT DATABASE 'exp';
Constraint Error: NOT NULL constraint failed: t.v
```

Expected: `(FORMAT CSV)` behaves exactly like `(FORMAT csv)`.

### OS:

Ubuntu 22.04.2 LTS, x86_64

### DuckDB Version:

v2.1.0-dev89158 (main, 1b4c3e54ba, built from source)

CLI

title: Deferred unique keys are treated as functional dependencies
body:
### What happens?

`ORDER BY` and window expressions drop keys that follow a `DEFERRED` primary key or `NOT NULL UNIQUE` constraint, even though those constraints are not checked until commit. Duplicate keys are visible inside the transaction, so the dropped key changes the result.

With the optimizer enabled, `ORDER BY a, b DESC` returns `10, 20` instead of `20, 10`. `rank() OVER (ORDER BY a, b DESC)` assigns both rows rank 1. `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY a, b)` returns 1 and 2 because the partition is reduced to `a` alone. `PRAGMA disable_optimizer` returns the correct results. The physical plan shows `Order By: #1 ASC` and `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY a)`.

An immediate primary key still makes a later key redundant, and that behavior is unchanged.

### To Reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE pk(a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY DEFERRED, b INTEGER);
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO pk VALUES (1, 10), (1, 20);

SELECT b FROM pk ORDER BY a, b DESC;

SELECT b, rank() OVER (ORDER BY a, b DESC) FROM pk ORDER BY b;

SELECT b, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY a, b) FROM pk ORDER BY b;

PRAGMA disable_optimizer;

SELECT b FROM pk ORDER BY a, b DESC;

SELECT b, rank() OVER (ORDER BY a, b DESC) FROM pk ORDER BY b;

SELECT b, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY a, b) FROM pk ORDER BY b;
```

Actual output with the optimizer enabled, then disabled:

```text
10
20

10	1
20	1

10	1
20	2

20
10

10	2
20	1

10	1
20	1
```

Expected output for both modes:

```text
20
10

10	2
20	1

10	1
20	1
```

`DEFERRED` means the constraint is checked at commit. DuckDB already returns both inserted rows from `SELECT` before `COMMIT` fails, so ordering and partitioning have to use the visible duplicates. The same error occurs for `NOT NULL UNIQUE DEFERRED`, a composite `PRIMARY KEY(...) DEFERRED`, and a prepared statement planned before the duplicates are inserted.

### Root cause

`RemoveRedundantOrderKeys` records every primary key, and every `UNIQUE` constraint whose columns are `NOT NULL`, as a functional dependency of a table scan. It then deletes later `ORDER BY` keys and reduces window partitions to that set. It does not look at `UniqueConstraint::IsDeferred()`. The storage layer skips deferred indexes when checking uniqueness, so the optimizer assumes a property the visible rows do not have.

### Environment

- OS: macOS 15.7.3, arm64.
- DuckDB version: `v2.1.0-dev84994`, untouched upstream `main` at `2bb5316a8b59904a5dc513b88b81b048e25bbcc5`.
- Client: native DuckDB CLI and SQLLogicTest, built with `GEN=ninja CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL=10 make release`.
- No external dataset or extension is required.

### Identity disclosure

- Full name: Henry Su.
- Affiliation: GitHub profile bio states “cs & math @ tamu”.

Public issues, pull requests, discussions, commits, blame, and tests were searched for deferred constraints, redundant order keys, and functional dependencies. #24000 and #24054, fixed by #25878, request dropping sort keys after an enforced unique prefix. They do not mention `DEFERRED`. No blocking overlap was found. Private internal tracker contents were not accessible.

title: Parquet file_index changes when join_filter_pushdown is enabled
body:
### What happens?

The same Parquet query returns a different `file_index` depending only on whether
`join_filter_pushdown` is enabled.

For an explicit input list `[A, B]`, a join that retains only B returns
`file_index = 0` with join-filter pushdown enabled, but `file_index = 1` with it
disabled. The matching data rows are unchanged.

The example below uses a runtime join filter on a Hive partition column.

I would expect B to retain its original index, 1, in both executions. An optimizer
toggle should not change a projected value. DuckDB's
[Parquet virtual-column test](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/3ff87f1ec7282ef44727e0e1d84237e88dd9a7b5/test/sql/copy/parquet/parquet_virtual_columns.test#L14)
also keeps the second file's index at 1 when filtering on `file_index`.

This reproduces in the standard DuckDB CLI, v2.0.0-dev3 (`ed599a4425`), with no
third-party extensions loaded. We also observed the same results in DuckDB v1.5.5
(`3ff87f1ec7`) built in the Sirius source tree with `SIRIUS_DISABLE=1`.

### To Reproduce

Run the following SQL in the DuckDB CLI from an empty, writable directory.
It generates all required Parquet files. No external data or third-party extension
is needed.

The other disabled optimizers keep the join shape fixed and prevent statistics
propagation from pruning files before execution. Between the two executions,
only `join_filter_pushdown` changes.

```sql
PRAGMA version;

COPY (
    SELECT part, i::INTEGER AS x
    FROM range(2) p(part), range(10000) t(i)
) TO 'file_index_repro' (FORMAT PARQUET, PARTITION_BY ('part'));

COPY (SELECT 1::BIGINT AS k)
TO 'selected_part.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET);

SET disabled_optimizers =
    'statistics_propagation,join_order,build_side_probe_side';

SELECT p.file_index, count(*) AS n, min(p.x) AS min_x, max(p.x) AS max_x
FROM read_parquet([
    'file_index_repro/part=0/*.parquet',
    'file_index_repro/part=1/*.parquet'
], hive_partitioning=true) p
JOIN read_parquet('selected_part.parquet', hive_partitioning=false) s
  ON p.part = s.k
GROUP BY p.file_index;

SET disabled_optimizers =
    'statistics_propagation,join_order,build_side_probe_side,join_filter_pushdown';

SELECT p.file_index, count(*) AS n, min(p.x) AS min_x, max(p.x) AS max_x
FROM read_parquet([
    'file_index_repro/part=0/*.parquet',
    'file_index_repro/part=1/*.parquet'
], hive_partitioning=true) p
JOIN read_parquet('selected_part.parquet', hive_partitioning=false) s
  ON p.part = s.k
GROUP BY p.file_index;

RESET disabled_optimizers;
```

Actual query output (`PRAGMA version`: `v2.0.0-dev3`, `ed599a4425`, `Development Version`):

```text
join_filter_pushdown enabled:
file_index | n     | min_x | max_x
0          | 10000 | 0     | 9999
```

title: NewVuln39: Silent NULL Row Drop in ON CONFLICT Inner-Conflict Detection
body:
### What happens?

In `CheckDistinctnessInternal()` (`src/execution/operator/persistent/physical_insert.cpp`, lines 311-339), NULL values in the conflict-target column are encoded as a fixed byte sequence by `CreateSortKeyHelpers::CreateSortKey`. Two NULL keys therefore produce identical sort keys and are flagged as an "inner conflict." `OnConflictHandling()` then removes the second row from `insert_chunk` without placing it into `update_chunk`, so for `DO NOTHING` the row is permanently lost with no error. The SQL standard requires that NULL does not conflict with NULL for UNIQUE constraints, meaning all NULL rows in the batch should be inserted.

### To Reproduce

Pure SQL: run directly from the duckdb CLI against an in-memory database.

```sql
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER, val INTEGER UNIQUE);

INSERT INTO t (id, val) VALUES (1, NULL), (2, NULL) ON CONFLICT (val) DO NOTHING;

SELECT COUNT(*) AS actual_count FROM t WHERE val IS NULL;

SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY id;

SELECT
    2 AS expected_null_rows,
    COUNT(*) AS actual_null_rows,
    CASE WHEN COUNT(*) = 2 THEN 'PASS: no bug' ELSE 'FAIL: silent row drop detected' END AS verdict
FROM t WHERE val IS NULL;
```

```sh
./build_asan/duckdb :memory: < poc.sql
```

```

│ actual_count │
│    int64     │
├──────────────┤
│            1 │
└──────────────┘
┌───────┬───────┐
│  id   │  val  │
│ int32 │ int32 │
├───────┼───────┤
│     1 │  NULL │
└───────┴───────┘

│ expected_null_rows │ actual_null_rows │            verdict             │
│       int32        │      int64       │            varchar             │
```

title: NewVuln44: TOCTOU Race in ALTER TABLE ADD PRIMARY KEY Allows NULL in PK Column
body:
### What happens?

`PhysicalCreateIndex::Finalize()` in `src/execution/operator/schema/physical_create_index.cpp` (lines 176–182) checks for NOT NULL violations only in T1's own local storage, missing rows committed by a concurrent transaction T2 between T1's `Sink()` scan and T1's `catalog.Alter()` call. The `DataTable` constructor in `src/storage/data_table.cpp` (line 175) contains a guard `if (constraint.type != ConstraintType::UNIQUE)` that short-circuits `VerifyNewConstraint` for PRIMARY KEY because PK is stored internally as `ConstraintType::UNIQUE`. The combined result is that a NULL row inserted and committed by T2 inside the race window is never verified, leaving a NULL value permanently resident in a PRIMARY KEY column after the `ALTER TABLE ADD PRIMARY KEY` transaction commits.

### To Reproduce

This requires a Python script using the `duckdb` Python module. Two separate `./build_asan/duckdb` CLI processes cannot share the same database file because DuckDB's exclusive file-lock allows only one writer at a time. The Python module enables multiple in-process connections to the same file, which is the only way to create the concurrent-writer scenario needed to trigger the race.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import duckdb
import threading
import os
import time

DB = "poc.duckdb"
ROWS = 3_000_000

def setup():
    conn = duckdb.connect(DB)
    conn.execute("CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER)")
    conn.execute(f"INSERT INTO t SELECT i FROM range(1, {ROWS + 1}) tbl(i)")
    conn.close()

def t1_alter():
    conn = duckdb.connect(DB)
    conn.execute("ALTER TABLE t ADD PRIMARY KEY(id)")
    conn.close()

def t2_insert_null(delay):
    time.sleep(delay)
    conn = duckdb.connect(DB)
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES(NULL)")
    conn.close()

for f in [DB, DB + ".wal"]:
    try:
        os.unlink(f)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        pass

setup()

th1 = threading.Thread(target=t1_alter)
th2 = threading.Thread(target=t2_insert_null, args=(0.01,))
th1.start()
th2.start()
th1.join()
th2.join()

conn = duckdb.connect(DB)
null_count = conn.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE id IS NULL").fetchone()[0]
print(f"NULL rows in PRIMARY KEY column: {null_count}")
if null_count > 0:
    print("RACE CONDITION VERIFIED: NULL exists in PRIMARY KEY column")
conn.close()

for f in [DB, DB + ".wal"]:
    try:
        os.unlink(f)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        pass
```

```sh
python3 poc_race.py
```

title: LEAD with a huge offset: default value or "Overflow in addition" depending on the row count / vector boundary
body:
Follow-up to #26392, spotted while reworking #24883.

`LEAD`/`LAG` computes the target row index once per outer-loop iteration in `WindowLeadLagExecutor::GetData` (`src/function/window/window_value_function.cpp`, `AddOperatorOverflowCheck`/`SubtractOperatorOverflowCheck` around line 730). When the index lands far outside the partition, the default/null fill then covers `MinValue(delta, target_limit)` rows in one go, so those rows never recompute the index. The first row of the *next* vector does — and by then `row_idx` has grown enough that `row_idx + offset` overflows:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT lead(i, 9223372036854775807) OVER () AS l FROM range(3) t(i)) WHERE l IS NULL;
-- 3

SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT lead(i, 9223372036854775807) OVER () AS l FROM range(5000) t(i)) WHERE l IS NULL;
-- Out of Range Error: Overflow in addition of INT64 (2048 + 9223372036854775807)!
```

Same binary, default `STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE=2048`: the query returns defaults while the whole partition fits into vectors whose first row still fits in int64, and throws once a vector starts at row 2048. The `STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE=2` CI jobs hit the same thing with as few as 3 rows (that is how it first surfaced in #24872's CI). `LAG(v, INT64_MIN)` overflows already at row 0, so its `Overflow in subtraction` error is stable across vector sizes — and asserted by the test added in #26392.

Whether a query errors should not depend on how the input happens to be cut into vectors (or on the row count). Two possible directions:

1. **Saturate** the index: compute with `TryAdd`/`TrySubtract` and treat an overflow as "outside the partition" → default value. This makes `LEAD(v, INT64_MAX)` uniformly return the default. This is what #24883 originally proposed; note it would also turn the `LAG(v, INT64_MIN)` error that #26392 just locked in into the default, so it needs a semantic call.
2. Keep the error, but make it uniform: detect that `row_idx + offset` cannot fit for the remaining rows, so small tables throw too instead of silently returning defaults.

Happy to send a PR for either direction.

title: IEJoin LEFT/RIGHT join crashes with INTERNAL Error when non-preserved side has a LIST column
body:
### What happens?

An IEJoin outer join (LEFT/RIGHT) whose non-preserved side carries a `LIST` column crashes with an internal error as soon as the list contents are consumed (writing it with CTAS, or `v[1]`):

```
INTERNAL Error: Attempted to dereference shared_ptr that is NULL!
```

After the error the database is invalidated, so every later statement in the same process fails.

Reproduced on the official v1.5.5 and v1.5.6 CLI. The current v2.0.0 nightly does not reproduce it (details below).

Stack trace (v1.5.6, CTAS):

```
duckdb::shared_ptr<duckdb::VectorBuffer, true>::operator->() const
duckdb::Vector::Flatten(unsigned long long)
duckdb::Vector::ToUnifiedFormat(unsigned long long, duckdb::UnifiedVectorFormat&)
duckdb::ListColumnData::Append(...)
duckdb::ColumnData::Append(...)
duckdb::RowGroup::Append(...)
duckdb::RowGroupCollection::Append(...)
duckdb::PhysicalInsert::Sink(...)
```

With `SELECT r.v[1] ...` it fails in `ListVector::GetEntry` / `ListExtractFunction` instead.

### To Reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE l AS SELECT g AS a FROM range(200000) t(g);
CREATE TABLE r AS SELECT g%2000 AS k, g%2000+3 AS k2, [g]::INT[] AS v FROM range(2000) t(g);
CREATE TABLE o AS SELECT l.a, r.v FROM l LEFT JOIN r ON l.a >= r.k AND l.a < r.k2;
-- INTERNAL Error: Attempted to dereference shared_ptr that is NULL!
```

The plan is `IE_JOIN` (Join Type: LEFT, conditions `a >= k`, `a < k2`).

With the default thread count this fails on every run. With `PRAGMA threads=1` this exact query succeeds (203998 rows, 6000 with a non-NULL `v`), but single-threaded execution does not avoid the bug in general. When no row matches, it also fails with one thread:

```sql
PRAGMA threads=1;
CREATE TABLE l AS SELECT g*2 AS a FROM range(200000) t(g);
CREATE TABLE r AS SELECT g*2+1 AS k, g*2+2 AS k2, [g]::INT[] AS v FROM range(2000) t(g);
-- still planned as IE_JOIN; no row matches (even a vs. [odd, odd+1))
CREATE TABLE o AS SELECT l.a, r.v FROM l LEFT JOIN r ON l.a >= r.k AND l.a < r.k2;   -- crashes
SELECT count(r.v[1]) FROM l LEFT JOIN r ON l.a >= r.k AND l.a < r.k2;               -- crashes
SELECT count(*), count(r.v) FROM l LEFT JOIN r ON l.a >= r.k AND l.a < r.k2;        -- OK: 200000 | 0
```

Results on v1.5.6:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Original query, threads = default / 2 / 4 / 8 | crash |
| Original query, threads = 1 | OK |
| LEFT, zero matches, threads = 1, CTAS or `v[1]` | crash |
| LEFT, zero matches, threads = 1, only `count(v)` | OK |
| RIGHT join, `LIST` on the left side, zero matches, threads = 1 | crash |
| LEFT, zero matches, threads = 1, `VARCHAR` instead of `INT[]` | OK |
| INNER join, threads = 8 | OK |

All of the above pass on nightly v2.0.0-alpha38195, still planned as IE_JOIN; threads=1 and threads=8 give identical results for the original query.

### Likely cause

From reading v1.5.6 `src/execution/operator/join/physical_iejoin.cpp`:

- `IEJoinLocalSourceState` creates its `unprojected` chunk with `InitializeEmpty(...)`. Its vectors have no data buffer and no LIST auxiliary buffer, and `DataChunk::Reset()` returns early because there are no vector caches.
- On the match path (`ResolveComplexJoin`), the columns are `Reference`d from the sorted payload, so they pick up valid buffers.
- On the outer path (`ExecuteLeftTask` / `ExecuteRightTask`), the other side's columns are only set with `SetVectorType(CONSTANT_VECTOR)` + `ConstantVector::SetNull(vec, true)`, which only flips the validity bit.

So a local source state that never processed a matching block emits a constant-NULL `LIST` vector without an auxiliary buffer. Readers that only check validity (`count(v)`) work; readers that touch the child vector (`ListColumnData::Append`, `ListVector::GetEntry`) dereference a null pointer. `VARCHAR` is not affected because it doesn't need that buffer. More threads make it much more likely that a task handling unmatched rows never saw a match, which is why the original query looks thread-dependent.

On `main` / the v2.0 line, `ExecuteLeftTask` calls `ConstantVector::SetNull(vec, count_t(count))` instead. When the vector has no buffer, that overload builds a full NULL constant via `Reference(vector, Value(type), count)`, which would explain why the v2.0 nightly works. That change appears to be part of the larger Vector API refactor and is not on `v1.5-variegata`.

Workaround on 1.5.x: carry only a row id through the range join, then fetch the list column with an equi-join:

```sql
SELECT x.a, r2.v
FROM (SELECT l.a, r.rid FROM l LEFT JOIN r ON l.a >= r.k AND l.a < r.k2) x
LEFT JOIN r r2 ON x.rid = r2.rid;
```

Would it be possible to backport a fix to v1.5? A targeted fix in `ExecuteLeftTask` / `ExecuteRightTask` (emit a proper NULL constant instead of only setting the validity bit) seems sufficient for 1.5.x.

title: date_trunc('week'/'isoyear') near the minimum date: signed integer overflow (UB) in date_t arithmetic
body:
### What happens?

`date_trunc('week', ...)` and `date_trunc('isoyear', ...)` on dates near the minimum date range trigger a signed integer overflow in `date_t::operator-` (`src/include/duckdb/common/types/date.hpp`). Under a UBSan build (`-fsanitize=undefined -fno-sanitize-recover`) the process aborts; in release builds this is undefined behavior.

`date_t::operator-` does raw `int32` arithmetic; the week/isoyear truncation paths subtract the weekday offset without a range check.

### To Reproduce

```sql
SELECT date_trunc('week', DATE '5877642-06-25 (BC)');
SELECT date_trunc('isoyear', DATE '5877642-06-25 (BC)');
```

On a UBSan build:

```
src/include/duckdb/common/types/date.hpp:58:28: runtime error: signed integer overflow: -2147483646 - 3 cannot be represented in type 'int32_t' (aka 'int')
```
