title: the approximate join-order search builds a plan that fatally invalidates the database
body:
### What happens?

A twelve-table join containing two `ANTI JOIN`s raises an internal error and then
**invalidates the database**: every subsequent statement on that connection,
`SELECT 1` included, fails until the process is restarted.

```
INTERNAL Error: Attempted to access index 1 within vector of size 1
```

```
FATAL Error: database has been invalidated because of a previous fatal error.
             The database must be restarted prior to being used again.
```

The query is valid — the same join returns `0` when the join order is chosen by
the exact search instead of the approximate one.

`approximate_join_order_threshold` selects which join-order search runs. It counts
tables in the join and **ships with a default of 12**, so a twelve-table join
reaches the approximate search with nothing configured — which is how this query
gets there. This makes an ordinary `SELECT` a way to take down a persistent
database process.

Two things narrow where to look, and I want to be careful not to over-claim:

* **The fault is at plan time, not execution.** `EXPLAIN` alone on the query below
  raises the same `INTERNAL Error` and invalidates the database.
* **`disabled_optimizers='join_order'` does *not* avoid it** (measured below), so
  the approximate search is the route by which the query reaches the fault at
  stock defaults rather than the sole cause. What does avoid it is disabling
  `filter_pushdown`.

Deterministic: identical at `threads=1`, `2` and `8`.

### To Reproduce


Nothing is `SET`; this is stock configuration. Cardinalities are load-bearing —
join order is cost-based, so the tables cannot be made uniform.

```sql
CREATE TABLE t0 AS SELECT i AS id, i % 17 AS k, i % 11 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 7 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 5000) s(i);
CREATE TABLE t1 AS SELECT i AS id, i % 7 AS k, i % 11 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 10 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 5) s(i);
CREATE TABLE t2 AS SELECT i AS id, i % 7 AS k, i % 5 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 10 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 50) s(i);
CREATE TABLE t3 AS SELECT i AS id, i % 17 AS k, i % 5 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 8 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 2000) s(i);
CREATE TABLE t4 AS SELECT i AS id, i % 97 AS k, i % 5 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 11 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 50) s(i);
CREATE TABLE t5 AS SELECT i AS id, i % 7 AS k, i % 11 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 10 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 500) s(i);
CREATE TABLE t6 AS SELECT i AS id, i % 3 AS k, i % 5 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 7 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 1) s(i);
CREATE TABLE t7 AS SELECT i AS id, i % 97 AS k, i % 5 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 10 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 5) s(i);
CREATE TABLE t8 AS SELECT i AS id, i % 7 AS k, i % 2 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 8 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 1) s(i);
CREATE TABLE t9 AS SELECT i AS id, i % 7 AS k, i % 2 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 7 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 5) s(i);
CREATE TABLE t10 AS SELECT i AS id, i % 7 AS k, i % 2 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 8 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 5) s(i);
CREATE TABLE t11 AS SELECT i AS id, i % 3 AS k, i % 5 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 13 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 5) s(i);

SELECT count(*) FROM t9 a0
  ANTI JOIN t3  a1  ON a1.id = a0.id
  JOIN      t1  a2  ON a2.id = a0.id
  JOIN      t4  a3  ON a3.id = a0.id
  ANTI JOIN t8  a4  ON a4.k  = a2.nk
  JOIN      t2  a5  ON a5.id = a0.id
  JOIN      t7  a6  ON a6.id = a2.id
  JOIN      t6  a7  ON a7.id = a2.id
  JOIN      t0  a8  ON a8.g  = a3.k
  JOIN      t5  a9  ON a9.id = a0.id
  JOIN      t10 a10 ON a10.id = a0.id
  JOIN      t11 a11 ON a11.id = a0.id;

SELECT 1;
```

Output:

```
INTERNAL Error: Attempted to access index 1 within vector of size 1

FATAL Error: Failed: database has been invalidated because of a previous fatal error. The database must be restarted prior to being used again.
Original error: "Attempted to access index 1 within vector of size 1"
```

Expected: `0`, then `1`.

### It is the approximate search, not the width of the join

Holding the query at **nine** tables and moving only the setting:

```sql
-- nine tables at stock defaults (9 < 12): exact search
SELECT count(*) FROM t9 a0 ANTI JOIN t3 a1 ON a1.id = a0.id JOIN t1 a2 ON a2.id = a0.id
  JOIN t4 a3 ON a3.id = a0.id ANTI JOIN t8 a4 ON a4.k = a2.nk JOIN t2 a5 ON a5.id = a0.id
  JOIN t7 a6 ON a6.id = a2.id JOIN t6 a7 ON a7.id = a2.id JOIN t0 a8 ON a8.g = a3.k;
-- 0

SET approximate_join_order_threshold = 9;   -- same nine tables, approximate search
-- ... same query ...
-- INTERNAL Error: Attempted to access index 1 within vector of size 1
```

Output on the commit above:

```
┌──────────────┐
│ count_star() │
├──────────────┤
│            0 │
└──────────────┘
INTERNAL Error: Attempted to access index 1 within vector of size 1
```

And from the other direction, padding the query at stock defaults:

| tables in the join | result at stock defaults |
|---|---|
| 9 | `0` |
| 10 | `0` |
| 11 | `0` |
| **12** | **`INTERNAL Error` → database invalidated** |

The cliff is exactly at the shipped default of 12. Both directions agree: the
exact search orders this join fine, the approximate one does not.

### What avoids it

Measured individually on the commit above:

```
SET threads=1                                      -> INTERNAL Error  (not parallelism-dependent)
SET disabled_optimizers='join_order'               -> INTERNAL Error  <-- does NOT avoid it
SET approximate_join_order_threshold = 10000       -> 0   (forces the exact search)
SET disabled_optimizers='filter_pushdown'          -> 0
SET disabled_optimizers='statistics_propagation'   -> 0
SET disabled_optimizers='column_lifetime'          -> 0
```

`filter_pushdown` is the load-bearing pass: every combination that includes it
returns `0`, and every combination without it fails, including
`disabled_optimizers='join_order'` on its own and on the nine-table form. So the
approximate search produces a plan shape that `filter_pushdown` then mishandles,
rather than the approximate search being wrong by itself — and the threshold
evidence above shows the exact search does not produce such a shape for this
query.

The whole thing happens before execution:

```
EXPLAIN SELECT count(*) FROM t9 a0 ANTI JOIN ... ;
-- INTERNAL Error: Attempted to access index 1 within vector of size 1
```

### Related

`Related: https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/23530` — the PR that added
`approximate_join_order_threshold`.

I am filing a second, **different** issue for the same query family: an
`ANTI JOIN` in a wide join that raises
`INTERNAL Error: Failed to bind column reference` instead. They are not
duplicates — different error, different severity, and that one occurs under the
*exact* search as well. I will cross-link them once both have numbers.


### OS:

Ubuntu 22.04.2 LTS, x86_64 (Linux 5.15.0-187-generic)

### DuckDB Version:

Built from source at `549c3c83fbefedd5fdf5426e8dbeaa4dc8fc56f2`on the `v2.0-cyanoptera` branch (DuckDB's default branch), also `81bc275dd6` (2026-09-10) and `ace2451f52` (2026-09-21).

### DuckDB Client:

CLI (`build/release/duckdb`), in-memory database

### Hardware:

_No response_

### Full Name:

Ke Han

### Affiliation:

Purdue University

### Did you include all relevant configuration (e.g., CPU architecture, Linux distribution) to reproduce the issue?

- [x] Yes, I have

### Did you include all code required to reproduce the issue?

- [x] Yes, I have

### Did you include all relevant data sets for reproducing the issue?

Yes

@@ -0,0 +1,46 @@

title: Wrong result: optimizer breaks De Morgan-equivalent predicates for NULL BOOLEAN
body:
### What happens?

DuckDB `v1.5.5` returns different results for two logically equivalent predicates involving a `NULL` Boolean value.

With the optimizer enabled, the first query returns the row while the second returns no rows. With `PRAGMA disable_optimizer`, both queries return the row.

### To Reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE t(c BOOLEAN);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (NULL);

SELECT *
FROM t
WHERE NOT ((c IS TRUE) AND (c < TRUE));

SELECT *
FROM t
WHERE (NOT (c IS TRUE)) OR (NOT (c < TRUE));
```

Output:

```text
First query: 1 row
Second query: 0 rows
```

Both queries should return 1 row.

Disabling the optimizer restores the expected result:

```sql
PRAGMA disable_optimizer;

SELECT *
FROM t
WHERE NOT ((c IS TRUE) AND (c < TRUE));

SELECT *
FROM t
WHERE (NOT (c IS TRUE)) OR (NOT (c < TRUE));
```

Output:

```text
First query: 1 row
Second query: 1 row
```

title: Released 1.4.x–1.5.x: WAL replay with interleaved ALTER TABLE / CREATE INDEX corrupts unbound index buffers → SIGSEGV on next indexed write (fixed on main & v1.5 branch; no release tag contains the fix)
body:
**Summary**

A WAL that interleaves `CREATE INDEX` / `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN` with row-data transactions poisons unbound index buffers during replay. On release builds (asserts off) the next index-maintaining write — or an automatic checkpoint — SIGSEGVs. On assert builds, opening the database fails during WAL replay with:

```
TransactionContext Error: Failure while replaying WAL file "...": Failed to commit: Assertion triggered
in file ".../unbound_index.cpp" on line 51: mapped_column_ids == mapped_column_ids_p
```

(Removing that assert exposes a second-layer guard, `column_data_collection.cpp:961 types == input_types`, also during replay — both fire at open, pinning the corruption to replay time.)

Affected: released 1.4.x and 1.5.x binaries — verified v1.4.4, v1.5.3, v1.5.4, v1.5.5 (aarch64 Linux). Layout-independent confirmation on v1.5.5: the fix's own regression tests (`test/sql/storage/wal/wal_replay_unbound_index_*.test`) fail 4/4 on a v1.5.5 build and pass 4/4 on the v1.5 branch tip.

Fix status: `9613097434` "fix buffering for unbound indexes" (#24038, 2026-07-21, first ships in v2.0.0) is on main AND already backported to the v1.5 maintenance branch by the author (#24326, merged 2026-07-31; I verified the content is present and its regression tests pass on the branch tip). **No 1.5.x release tag contains it** (checked v1.5.0–v1.5.5) — v1.5.5 was tagged the day the fix landed on main, before the backport. Filing so the crash is publicly searchable and to note the release gap: a v1.5.6 cut from the current branch would close it.

**Minimal reproduction (from scratch; deterministic SIGSEGV on 1.4.4)**

```sql
-- process 1
PRAGMA disable_checkpoint_on_shutdown;
CREATE TABLE t(a BIGINT, b VARCHAR);
INSERT INTO t SELECT i, 'x'||i FROM range(1) s(i);
CREATE INDEX idx_a ON t(a);
BEGIN; INSERT INTO t SELECT i+100, 'y'||i FROM range(1) s(i); COMMIT;

-- process 2 (replays the WAL)
PRAGMA disable_checkpoint_on_shutdown;
ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c BIGINT;
CREATE INDEX idx_c ON t(c);
BEGIN; INSERT INTO t(a,b) SELECT i+200, 'z'||i FROM range(1) s(i); COMMIT;

-- process 3 (replays again) — any index-maintaining write crashes
PRAGMA disable_checkpoint_on_shutdown;
INSERT INTO t VALUES (999, 'q', 1);   -- SIGSEGV
```

Read-only opens never crash. Two un-checkpointed close/reopen cycles and an `ALTER ADD COLUMN` between the two index creations are required; INSERT-only works (no DELETE needed); on assert builds process 3 fails at OPEN with the message above. Note: whether the minimal 3-process variant *crashes* on a given 1.5.x build is heap-layout dependent (on 1.5.x the corrupted state is created silently and crashes on other indexed-write workloads — e.g. a larger interleaved workload crashes all of v1.5.3–v1.5.5 deterministically; the regression-test failures above are the layout-independent evidence).

**Root cause**

Replayed `CREATE INDEX` leaves an `UnboundIndex` whose buffered replays latch `mapped_column_ids` (union of all indexed columns at buffering time) on the first buffered chunk — guarded only by `D_ASSERT`. `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` + `CREATE INDEX` inside the same WAL grows that union between buffered operations, so later chunks carry a different layout and are silently appended into the narrow buffer (the `types == input_types` guard is also assert-only). On the next bind, `BoundIndex::ApplyBufferedReplays` reads `mapped_column_ids[col_idx]` beyond the latched vector → garbage column id → `table_chunk.data[col_id].Reference(...)` → wild access. (A shrinking union — DROP INDEX/COLUMN mid-WAL — would be a real heap OOB rather than silent truncation.)

Automatic checkpoints trigger the same bind, so an automatic checkpoint alone can crash a poisoned database without any follow-up statement.

**Verification data**

- v1.4.4/1.5.3/1.5.4/1.5.5 release-semantics builds: deterministic SIGSEGV on the interleaved workload; v2.0.0-dev clean.
- Main bisect: parent `8d15d0be8d` crashes, `9613097434` clean.
- v1.5 branch tip: repro passes, 4/4 regression tests pass, `test/sql/storage/` 554 cases / 86,300 assertions pass.

title: [Wrong result] Streaming LEAD followed by UNNEST duplicates the final row
body:
### What happens?

A query that applies `UNNEST` downstream of a streaming `LEAD` window returns one extra row and an incorrect aggregate result.

The input to `LEAD` contains one row. The default value makes `x` equal to `7`, and `range(200000)` should expand that row to exactly 200,000 rows. DuckDB instead returns 200,001 rows with a sum of 1,400,007.

This reproduces with default settings on both the current stable release and the latest `main` commit. It also reproduces consistently with one thread. No external data or extensions are involved.

### To Reproduce

Run the following query in DuckDB:

```sql
SELECT count(*), sum(x)
FROM (
    SELECT unnest(range(200000)) AS u, x
    FROM (
        SELECT lead(i, 1, 7) OVER () AS x
        FROM range(1) t(i)
    )
    LIMIT 200001
);
```

title: Bug95: RemapList leaves list_entry_t array uninitialized, causing D_ASSERT crash in allocator
body:
### What happens?

In `src/function/scalar/struct/remap_struct.cpp`, `RemapList()` (lines 136–172) handles a `CONSTANT_VECTOR` list child by copying only `result[0]` via `memcpy`, while leaving `result[1..result_size-1]` as stale heap garbage — without ever calling `result.SetVectorType(VectorType::CONSTANT_VECTOR)` to signal that only index 0 is meaningful. When the enclosing struct is a `FLAT_VECTOR` (row-varying column reference) but the `LIST` sub-field is `CONSTANT_VECTOR` (pure literal expression), and a nested-remap mapping forces the recursive `RemapNested` → `RemapList` path, those garbage `list_entry_t{offset, length}` values propagate downstream. Downstream consumers use the garbage offset/length to size a memory allocation, tripping `D_ASSERT(size < MAXIMUM_ALLOC_SIZE)` in `Allocator::AllocateData` and crashing the process with an `INTERNAL Error`; in a release build (where `D_ASSERT` is compiled out) the same path produces an out-of-bounds heap read or OOM.


### To Reproduce

This is triggered entirely by SQL, with no external data files.

```sql
SELECT remap_struct(
    {'id': i, 'lst': list_value(1, 2, 3)},
    NULL::STRUCT(id INTEGER, lst2 INTEGER[]),
    {'id': 'id', 'lst2': ROW('lst', {'list': 'list'})},
    NULL
) FROM range(5) tbl(i);
```

```sh
    NULL::STRUCT(id INTEGER, lst2 INTEGER[]),

EOF
```

title: Hash Aggregate Can Skip Required Repartition
body:
### What happens?

This is similar in nature to the hash join issue https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/25206

The external hash aggregate uses the temporary memory reservation to decide whether a local aggregate hash table should switch to external mode / repartition.

Code path:
```
RadixPartitionedHashTable::Sink
  -> MaybeRepartition
  -> total_size > gstate.GetThreadLimit()
```
where:
```
RadixHTGlobalSinkState::GetThreadLimit
  -> temporary_memory_state->GetReservation() / number_of_threads / 10 * 8
```
When the local HT grows beyond the per-thread limit, MaybeRepartition updates the temporary memory state:
```
MaybeRepartition
  -> TemporaryMemoryState::SetMinimumReservation(...)
  -> TemporaryMemoryState::SetRemainingSizeAndUpdateReservation(...)
  -> TemporaryMemoryManager::UpdateState(...)
```
However, TemporaryMemoryManager::UpdateState can hit the overshot branch:
```
if (reservation - temporary_memory_state.GetReservation() + lower_bound >= memory_limit) {
    // We overshot. Set reservation equal to the minimum
    SetReservation(temporary_memory_state, lower_bound);
}
```
Here, lower_bound can be the operator minimum reservation. This reservation is not necessarily a real physical memory grant: total reservations can still exceed the global memory limit. In other
words, GetReservation() can represent an overcommitted logical budget.

Problem:

MaybeRepartition then uses this possibly overcommitted reservation to compute GetThreadLimit(). As a result, the aggregate can incorrectly decide that the local hash table is still within its memory budget and skip external repartitioning.

This can produce an inaccurate repartition decision:

- external mode may be triggered too late or not at all
- radix bits may be chosen based on an overcommitted reservation
- partitions can remain larger than what can actually be processed safely
- later Combine / Finalize / GetData can hit an avoidable OOM


### To Reproduce

```
# name: test/sql/aggregate/external/grouping_sets_repartition_reservation.test_slow
# description: Test external hash aggregate repartitioning with many grouping sets under low memory
# group: [external]

require noforcestorage

require skip_reload

require 64bit

# This test relies on the default vector size and block size for the memory threshold.
require vector_size 2048

require block_size 262144

statement ok
SET temp_directory='__TEST_DIR__/grouping_sets_repartition_reservation'

statement ok
SET threads=4

statement ok
SET memory_limit='140MB'

statement ok
SET preserve_insertion_order=false

# Avoid compressed materialization hiding the intended hash aggregate memory pressure.
statement ok
SET disabled_optimizers='compressed_materialization'

query I
WITH t AS (
	SELECT concat(i::VARCHAR, repeat('x', 64)) AS g
	FROM range(1000000) r(i)
)
SELECT count(*)
FROM (
	SELECT g, count(*) AS c
	FROM t
	GROUP BY CUBE(g, g, g, g)
) q
----
15000001

```

title: NewVuln12: Stack Overflow via Unbounded Recursion on Nested LIST Types
body:
### What happens?

`ExtractCollationFromType()` and `ApplyCollationToType()` in `src/function/function_binder.cpp` (lines 662–718) recurse unconditionally on `LIST` child types with no depth counter or guard. When `list_contains` is bound with a deeply nested `LIST(LIST(...INTEGER...))` argument, the collation-handling path invokes `ExtractCollationFromType()` for every nesting level. In practice the expression-depth guard fires first and attempts to build a diagnostic string through `TypeExpression::ToString()`, which carries the same unbounded LIST recursion, exhausting the thread stack and crashing the process with an ASan `stack-overflow` before `ExtractCollationFromType()` is even reached. Both call paths share the same root cause (CWE-674) and the same fix.

### To Reproduce

This PoC requires first using a Python script to generate a SQL file containing a deeply nested LIST type expression, because the SQL contains approximately 5000 bracket pairs and cannot be written by hand.

```python
# gen_poc.py
depth = 5000
brackets = "[]" * depth
sql = (
    "SET max_expression_depth = 300000;\n"
    f"SELECT list_contains(CAST(NULL AS INTEGER{brackets}), 1);\n"
)
with open("poc.sql", "w") as f:
    f.write(sql)
```

```sh
python3 gen_poc.py
./build_asan/duckdb :memory: < poc.sql
```

title: Incorrect results: hash join silently drops rows when the build side spills to disk
body:
### What happens?

A hash join whose build side spills to disk silently returns a strict subset of
its rows. With a 60 MB memory limit, a semi join that must return 3,000,000 rows
returns 480,000 — no error, no warning. The join key values that survive are
exactly those whose partitions were built in the first round of the external
build; every row of the remaining keys is discarded by a Bloom filter that was
pushed into the probe-side scan before the later rounds ran.

INNER, SEMI, EXISTS and `IN (subquery)` are all affected. Released 1.5.5 is correct.

### To Reproduce

```sql
SET threads=1;

-- 3,000,000 rows, 25 distinct keys, 120,000 rows per key.
CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT (i%25)::int AS a FROM range(3000000) tbl(i);
CREATE TABLE u AS SELECT (i%25)::int AS b FROM range(3000000) tbl(i);

-- Any limit small enough that the build side does not fit; the join then goes external.
SET memory_limit='60MB';

SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE a IN (SELECT b FROM u);

┌──────────────┐
│ count_star() │
│    int64     │
├──────────────┤
│       480000 │
└──────────────┘

SET disabled_optimizers='join_filter_pushdown';
SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE a IN (SELECT b FROM u);

┌────────────────┐
│  count_star()  │
│     int64      │
├────────────────┤
│    3000000     │
│ (3.00 million) │
└────────────────┘


```

Every row of `t` has 120,000 matches in `u`, so the semi join must return all
3,000,000 rows of `t`.

### OS:

Ubuntu 22.04.2 LTS, x86_64, kernel 5.15.0-187-generic

main, commit 8bc48eb3fe36f13b5e57e5e136c3ba85cc7d74d4

title: Casting `variant_extract(v, 'k')` to JSON on a shredded VARIANT column parses the string instead of serializing it: `"true"` becomes the boolean `true`, `"x"` raises Malformed JSON
body:
### What happens?


On a VARIANT column whose row group has been **shredded** (at or above
`variant_minimum_shredding_size`, default 30 000 rows), `variant_extract(v, 'k')::JSON` for a
string-valued key returns the string's *contents parsed as JSON* rather than the string as a
JSON string:

| stored value of `k` | `variant_extract(v,'k')::JSON`, unshredded | same, shredded |
|---|---|---|
| `"x"` | `"x"` | **`Conversion Error: Malformed JSON at byte 0 of input: unexpected character.  Input: "x"`** |
| `"true"` | `"true"` (`json_type` = VARCHAR) | **`true`** (`json_type` = BOOLEAN) |
| `"1"` | `"1"` | **`1`** |
| `"null"` | `"null"` | **`null`** |

So a string that happens to be valid JSON silently changes type, and one that is not raises.
`variant_typeof(variant_extract(v,'k'))` still says `VARCHAR` on the shredded side, and
`variant_extract(v,'k')::VARCHAR` returns the string correctly; only the JSON cast of the
extraction is affected. The whole-document cast `v::JSON` is correct too.

The cause is the optimizer's pushdown of `variant_extract` + cast into the storage scan
(`RemoveUnusedColumns`): for a fully shredded column the extracted key is read straight from the
shredded typed sub-column, which is a plain `VARCHAR`, and the pushed-down cast becomes
`CAST(VARCHAR AS JSON)` — which *parses* — instead of the `VARIANT → JSON` cast, which
*serializes*. Details and the three fingerprints (`TRY_CAST`, a subquery, and
`disabled_optimizers='unused_columns'` all give the right answer) are under "Notes".

Released 1.5.6 is correct on every query below, so this is a regression in the development
branches.


### To Reproduce


Nothing is set; `variant_minimum_shredding_size` stays at its default of 30 000. One row more
flips the answer.

```sql
ATTACH 'x.db' (STORAGE_VERSION 'v1.5.0');
USE x;

CREATE TABLE small(id INTEGER, v VARIANT);
INSERT INTO small SELECT i, '{"a":"x"}'::JSON::VARIANT FROM range(29999) tbl(i);
CREATE TABLE big(id INTEGER, v VARIANT);
INSERT INTO big   SELECT i, '{"a":"x"}'::JSON::VARIANT FROM range(30000) tbl(i);
CHECKPOINT;   -- shredding is decided when the row group is written

SELECT (variant_extract(v,'a')::JSON)::VARCHAR FROM small LIMIT 1;
SELECT (variant_extract(v,'a')::JSON)::VARCHAR FROM big   LIMIT 1;
```

Output (`v2.0-cyanoptera` 097ee1d34a; `main` d6b403d382 is identical; re-checked identical on `v2.0-cyanoptera` 35e46672d1 and `main` 4a0fa3d797, 2026-10-01):

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ CAST(CAST(variant_extract(v, 'a') AS "JSON") AS VARCHAR) │
│                         varchar                          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ "x"                                                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Conversion Error: Malformed JSON at byte 0 of input: unexpected character.  Input: "x"
```

The silent half — a stored string that happens to parse — at the same threshold:

```sql
CREATE TABLE small2(id INTEGER, v VARIANT);
INSERT INTO small2 SELECT i, '{"k":"true"}'::JSON::VARIANT FROM range(29999) tbl(i);
CREATE TABLE big2(id INTEGER, v VARIANT);
INSERT INTO big2   SELECT i, '{"k":"true"}'::JSON::VARIANT FROM range(30000) tbl(i);
CHECKPOINT;

SELECT (variant_extract(v,'k')::JSON)::VARCHAR AS val,
       json_type(variant_extract(v,'k')::JSON)  AS json_type,
       variant_typeof(variant_extract(v,'k'))   AS variant_type
FROM small2 LIMIT 1;
SELECT (variant_extract(v,'k')::JSON)::VARCHAR AS val,
       json_type(variant_extract(v,'k')::JSON)  AS json_type,
       variant_typeof(variant_extract(v,'k'))   AS variant_type
FROM big2 LIMIT 1;
```

```
| val    | json_type | variant_type |      <- 29,999 rows
| "true" | VARCHAR   | VARCHAR      |
| val    | json_type | variant_type |      <- 30,000 rows
| true   | BOOLEAN   | VARCHAR      |
```

Shredding directly gets there with one row per value:

```sql
ATTACH 'y.db' (STORAGE_VERSION 'v1.5.0');
USE y;
SET variant_minimum_shredding_size = 1;
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER, v VARIANT);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, '{"a":"x"}'::JSON::VARIANT), (2, '{"a":"true"}'::JSON::VARIANT),
                     (3, '{"a":"1"}'::JSON::VARIANT), (4, '{"a":"null"}'::JSON::VARIANT);
CHECKPOINT;

SELECT id, variant_extract(v,'a')::VARCHAR AS as_varchar,
       variant_typeof(variant_extract(v,'a')) AS vtype, (v::JSON)::VARCHAR AS whole_doc FROM t ORDER BY id;
SELECT id, (variant_extract(v,'a')::JSON)::VARCHAR AS as_json,
       json_type(variant_extract(v,'a')::JSON) AS jtype FROM t WHERE id IN (2,3,4) ORDER BY id;
SELECT id, (variant_extract(v,'a')::JSON)::VARCHAR AS as_json FROM t WHERE id = 1;
```

```
| id | as_varchar | vtype   | whole_doc    |
| 1  | x          | VARCHAR | {"a":"x"}    |
| 2  | true       | VARCHAR | {"a":"true"} |
| 3  | 1          | VARCHAR | {"a":"1"}    |
| 4  | null       | VARCHAR | {"a":"null"} |
Conversion Error: Malformed JSON at byte 0 of input: unexpected character.  Input: "x"
Conversion Error: Malformed JSON at byte 0 of input: unexpected character.  Input: "x"
```

(The second statement fails as a whole because row 1 is in the table; on a table without the
`"x"` row it returns `true`/BOOLEAN, `1`/UBIGINT, `null`/NULL — the first table above shows the
same thing at 30 000 rows.)

`CHECKPOINT` is required in every case: before it the column is still unshredded in memory and
the cast is correct.

### Expected

The JSON cast of an extracted string is the JSON *string*, whatever the row group's layout —

title: ClientContext::Destroy() can std::terminate() the process - no safe way to drop a connection after a FATAL mid-transaction
body:
## What

Once a FATAL/INTERNAL error invalidates a `DatabaseInstance` (`ValidChecker::Invalidate`), every subsequent statement is refused, ROLLBACK included:

> database has been invalidated because of a previous fatal error

If that FATAL happened inside an explicit (non-autocommit) transaction, there is no way to cleanly dispose of the connection afterward:

- Calling `Connection::Rollback()` yourself throws immediately, because it's just another statement and the instance is invalidated.
- Simply dropping the connection instead doesn't help either: `ClientContext::~ClientContext()` calls `Destroy()`, which — because `transaction.HasActiveTransaction()` is still true and the transaction isn't autocommit — calls `transaction.Rollback(nullptr)` itself, with no try/catch:

  https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/08e34c447bae34eaee3723cac61f2878b6bdf787/src/main/client_context.cpp#L198-L207

`TransactionContext::Rollback()` is designed to make a failure observable: it catches the underlying exception, then deliberately re-throws it via `ErrorData::Throw()` so a caller can see it:

  https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/08e34c447bae34eaee3723cac61f2878b6bdf787/src/transaction/transaction_context.cpp#L81-L103

For a catalog/storage extension that implements `Transaction::Rollback()` by issuing further SQL against its own connection (as DuckLake — github.com/duckdb/ducklake — does, against its metadata store), that inner statement is refused for the same invalidated-database reason, so `TransactionContext::Rollback()`'s rethrow fires. Because `Destroy()` doesn't catch it and `~ClientContext()` is an implicit `noexcept` destructor, the exception reaching it calls `std::terminate()` and aborts the whole process — not just the one connection.

`ClientContext::EndQueryInternal()`, the normal query-end path, avoids exactly this: it wraps the equivalent `Commit()`/`Rollback()` call in try/catch and turns a failure into a returned `ErrorData` instead of letting it propagate:

  https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/08e34c447bae34eaee3723cac61f2878b6bdf787/src/main/client_context.cpp#L258-L309

`Destroy()` doesn't. This is the same bug class as #22860 (`DuckTransaction::Commit()`'s unprotected `RevertCommit()` calls, fixed by #23298) — a different call site that fix didn't cover, and one that's reachable through the ordinary, documented "invalidated database" error path rather than needing a second independent failure.

## Impact

Any embedder that (reasonably) reacts to a FATAL/INTERNAL error by discarding the connection and opening a fresh one crashes the entire process instead, whenever the error happened mid-explicit-transaction on a catalog whose Rollback is externally observable (a real statement against another connection/store, not just in-process bookkeeping). There is currently no API-level way to dispose of such a connection without risking this.

## Suggested fix

Wrap the `transaction.Rollback(nullptr)` call in `Destroy()` in a try/catch mirroring `EndQueryInternal()`'s — there's no result object to report into at teardown, so the error can simply be swallowed/logged. Happy to send a PR along these lines if useful.

## Version

Confirmed present on `duckdb/duckdb@08e34c4` (current main at time of writing). The crash was originally observed against an older release; the source defect itself is unchanged on current main.

title: COPY TO PARQUET silently loses the sign of negative zero once the column is dictionary-encoded
body:
### What happens?


Writing a `DOUBLE` (or `FLOAT`) column that contains both `-0.0` and `+0.0` to Parquet
loses the sign of every zero, as soon as the writer chooses dictionary encoding. The
dictionary deduplicates values with floating-point `==`, and `-0.0 == +0.0` is true in
IEEE 754 even though the two have different bit patterns, so both signs collapse onto
whichever entry was inserted first.

Nothing errors and nothing warns, and **the file on disk is wrong** — not merely misread.
Written uncompressed so the raw bytes are visible:

```
4-row file (PLAIN, 240 B):            -0.0 bit pattern 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 80 present -> True
5-row file (PLAIN_DICTIONARY, 294 B): -0.0 bit pattern 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 80 present -> False
```

The switch to dictionary encoding is driven by the column's distinct-value count, so for a
column of zeros it happens at **5 rows**. A test that writes four rows passes; a test that
writes five loses data.

Reproduces on current `main` and on released **1.5.5**.


### To Reproduce

No settings are changed; only the number of rows varies.

```sql
-- 4 rows: PLAIN encoding, correct
COPY (SELECT CASE WHEN i % 2 = 0 THEN 0.0::DOUBLE ELSE -0.0::DOUBLE END AS c
      FROM range(4) t(i))
  TO '/tmp/z4.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET);
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE signbit(c))     AS negative_zeros,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT signbit(c)) AS positive_zeros
FROM read_parquet('/tmp/z4.parquet');           -- 2 / 2, correct

-- 5 rows: PLAIN_DICTIONARY, the signs are gone
COPY (SELECT CASE WHEN i % 2 = 0 THEN 0.0::DOUBLE ELSE -0.0::DOUBLE END AS c
      FROM range(5) t(i))
  TO '/tmp/z5.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET);
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE signbit(c))     AS negative_zeros,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT signbit(c)) AS positive_zeros
FROM read_parquet('/tmp/z5.parquet');           -- 0 / 5, wrong

-- which encoding was used
SELECT DISTINCT encodings FROM parquet_metadata('/tmp/z4.parquet');   -- PLAIN
SELECT DISTINCT encodings FROM parquet_metadata('/tmp/z5.parquet');   -- PLAIN_DICTIONARY
```

### Expected

The signs survive the round trip at every row count, as they do at 4 rows:

```
 negative_zeros │ positive_zeros
              2 │              3      -- for the 5-row file
```

### Actual

```
 negative_zeros │ positive_zeros
              0 │              5
```

title: Vuln71: Stack Overflow via Deeply Nested WITH RECURSIVE Subqueries
body:
### What happens?

`RecursiveCTENode::Copy()`, `RecursiveCTENode::ToString()`, and `Binder::BindNode(RecursiveCTENode&)` all recurse directly through the `left` and `right` child `QueryNode` fields with no depth guard. When those children are themselves `RecursiveCTENode` objects, reachable by nesting `WITH RECURSIVE` blocks inside subqueries that serve as anchor terms of outer recursive CTEs, the call depth grows proportionally to nesting level. At approximately 5 000 levels, the accumulated stack frames exhaust the default 8 MB thread stack, causing a fatal stack overflow that crashes the host process unconditionally.

### To Reproduce

**Step 1 — Generate `poc.sql`:**

```python
N = 5000

inner = "SELECT 1"
for i in range(N):
    name = f"r{i}"
    inner = f"(WITH RECURSIVE {name} AS (({inner}) UNION ALL SELECT 1 FROM {name}) SELECT * FROM {name})"

sql = f"SELECT * FROM {inner};\n"

with open("poc.sql", "w") as f:
    f.write(sql)
```

**Step 2 — Run:**

```sh
python3 gen.py          # produces poc.sql
./build/debug/duckdb < poc.sql
```

**Step 3 — Observed ASan output:**


title: ManualVuln26 COPY BLOB COMPRESSION Option Without Value Causes Out-of-Bounds Vector Access in WriteBlobBind
body:
### What happens?

`WriteBlobBind` (`src/function/copy_blob.cpp`, line 46) iterates over `input.info.options` and reads `option_values[0]` unconditionally for the `compression` option. The `option_values` vector is populated by `BindCopyOption` (`src/planner/binder/statement/bind_copy.cpp`, lines 706-710): when a COPY option is written without any argument expression (e.g. `COMPRESSION` with no `= 'zstd'` part), `BindCopyOption` receives a null `unique_ptr<ParsedExpression>` and returns an empty `vector<Value>` immediately. That empty vector is stored into `input.info.options["compression"]`, so when `WriteBlobBind` reaches `option_values[0]`, the vector has size 0 and the access is an unconditional out-of-bounds heap read.

The violated invariant is that every COPY format bind function must guard against a zero-length `option_values` before indexing into it. Parquet already enforces this with `if (option_values.size() != 1) throw BinderException(...)` at `parquet_extension.cpp:183`, but the BLOB handler has no such guard. In both the release and debug builds the out-of-bounds access is caught by DuckDB's own bounds-checked `duckdb::vector` and surfaces as "INTERNAL Error: Attempted to access index 0 within vector of size 0".

### To Reproduce

Reproducible directly via plain SQL from the DuckDB CLI client, no external file or script required.

SQL script (`manual26_blob_compression_no_value.sql`):

```sql
COPY (SELECT 'test'::BLOB AS data) TO '/tmp/test.bin' (FORMAT BLOB, COMPRESSION);
```

title: Partitioned COPY with ROW_GROUP_SIZE_BYTES silently merges distinct string partitions
body:
### What happens?

`COPY ... PARTITION_BY` silently writes rows into the wrong partition when `ROW_GROUP_SIZE_BYTES` is enabled. Two string date partitions with 2,048 rows each become one partition with 4,096 rows; no error is raised and the total row count remains correct.

Reproduced on the [official October 7 cp311 Linux wheel](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-python/actions/runs/37645168698/artifacts/11495154732), package `2.0.0.dev2610071535`, core `df47ba32d9` (`v2.0.0-dev86676`). The same reproduction passes on published `1.5.6` and `2.0.0.dev2610011535`.

### To reproduce

Only DuckDB and synthetic data are needed:

```python
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
import duckdb

with TemporaryDirectory() as root, duckdb.connect(config={"threads": 1}) as c:
    c.execute("SET preserve_insertion_order=false")
    query = """
        SELECT repeat('w', 1024) AS name, '2026' AS year, '07' AS month,
               CASE WHEN i < 2048 THEN '07' ELSE '08' END AS day
        FROM range(4096) t(i)
    """
    for limited in [False, True]:
        dest = f"{root}/{limited}"
        options = ", ROW_GROUP_SIZE_BYTES '50MiB'" if limited else ""
        c.execute(f"""
            COPY ({query}) TO ?
            (FORMAT PARQUET, PARTITION_BY(year,month,day),
             PRESERVE_ORDER false{options})
        """, [dest])
        print(limited, c.execute("""
            SELECT day, count(*) FROM read_parquet(?, hive_partitioning=true)
            GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL
        """, [dest + "/**/*.parquet"]).fetchall())
```

Actual:

```text
False [('07', 2048), ('08', 2048)]
True [('07', 4096)]
```

Expected: both cases return `[('07', 2048), ('08', 2048)]`.

### Environment

Ubuntu 22.04.5, x86_64; Python 3.11.13.


Workaround: omit `ROW_GROUP_SIZE_BYTES`.

title: ORDER BY changes -0.0 to +0.0 for DOUBLE values
body:
### What happens?

Sorting a `DOUBLE` column with `ORDER BY` changes a negative zero
(`-0.0`) into positive zero (`+0.0`).

The change is observable through both `signbit(v)` and subsequent
floating-point arithmetic:

- before sorting: `signbit(v) = true` and `1.0 / v = -Infinity`
- after sorting: `signbit(v) = false` and `1.0 / v = Infinity`

The affected row is identified by an explicit `id`, so this is not
caused by a change in the output ordering of the two equal zero values.

Reproduced with DuckDB v1.5.5 and v1.5.6.dev32 using an isolated
connection.

### To Reproduce

Run the following SQL in a fresh DuckDB connection:

```sql
CREATE TEMP TABLE srs_zero_probe(id INTEGER, v DOUBLE);

INSERT INTO srs_zero_probe VALUES
    (1, '-0.0'),
    (2, '0.0');

WITH q AS MATERIALIZED (
    SELECT id, v
    FROM srs_zero_probe
)
SELECT id, v, signbit(v), 1.0 / v
FROM q
ORDER BY id;
```

The baseline result preserves negative zero:

```text
1  -0.0  true   -Infinity
2   0.0  false   Infinity
```

Now sort the intermediate result by the `DOUBLE` column:

```sql
WITH q AS MATERIALIZED (
    SELECT id, v
    FROM srs_zero_probe
    ORDER BY v, id
)
SELECT id, v, signbit(v), 1.0 / v
FROM q
ORDER BY id;
```

Actual result:

```text
1  0.0  false  Infinity
2  0.0  false  Infinity
```

Expected result:

```text
1  -0.0  true   -Infinity
2   0.0  false   Infinity
```

The value associated with `id = 1` changes from negative zero to
positive zero after `ORDER BY v`. Thus, this is not only a formatting
difference: the result of `signbit(v)` changes from `true` to `false`,
and `1.0 / v` changes from `-Infinity` to `Infinity`.

### OS:

Ubuntu 20.04 x86_64

### DuckDB Version:

v1.5.5 and v1.5.6.dev32

### DuckDB Client:

CLI

x86_64

title: a wide join containing an ANTI JOIN mis-binds its columns
body:
### What happens?


An eight-table join containing one `ANTI JOIN`, aggregated with
`count(DISTINCT …)`, fails to bind after the join-order optimizer rewrites it:

```
INTERNAL Error: Failed to bind column reference "k" [0.1] (bindings: {#[21.0]})
```

This is not a wrong answer — it is a hard failure on a query that is plainly
valid, and *valid* is not a judgement call here: **the same query returns `0`
under a different join order**. Per DuckDB's own convention an `INTERNAL Error`
is an invariant the engine expected to hold, so this is a bug by definition.

It fails at stock defaults. It is not parallelism-dependent (`threads=1` fails
identically).

### To Reproduce


Nothing is `SET`. Cardinalities are load-bearing — join order is cost-based, so
the 1-row and 500-row tables cannot be made uniform.

```sql
CREATE TABLE t0  AS SELECT i AS id, i % 3  AS k, i % 11 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 9  = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 1)   s(i);
CREATE TABLE t1  AS SELECT i AS id, i % 17 AS k, i % 11 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 8  = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 500) s(i);
CREATE TABLE t4  AS SELECT i AS id, i % 17 AS k, i % 5  AS g, CASE WHEN i % 7  = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 500) s(i);
CREATE TABLE t7  AS SELECT i AS id, i % 7  AS k, i % 2  AS g, CASE WHEN i % 12 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 1)   s(i);
CREATE TABLE t8  AS SELECT i AS id, i % 97 AS k, i % 2  AS g, CASE WHEN i % 11 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 1)   s(i);
CREATE TABLE t9  AS SELECT i AS id, i % 7  AS k, i % 2  AS g, CASE WHEN i % 9  = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 1)   s(i);
CREATE TABLE t10 AS SELECT i AS id, i % 97 AS k, i % 5  AS g, CASE WHEN i % 8  = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 500) s(i);
CREATE TABLE t11 AS SELECT i AS id, i % 17 AS k, i % 11 AS g, CASE WHEN i % 12 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE i % 23 END AS nk FROM range(0, 500) s(i);

SELECT count(DISTINCT a0.k)
FROM t1 a0
     JOIN      t0  a3  ON a3.id  = a0.nk
     ANTI JOIN t7  a5  ON a5.id  = a0.nk
     JOIN      t10 a6  ON a6.id  = a3.id
     JOIN      t4  a7  ON a7.id  = a6.id
     JOIN      t8  a8  ON a8.g   = a3.nk
     JOIN      t11 a10 ON a10.id = a3.id
     JOIN      t9  a11 ON a11.id = a7.id
WHERE a10.id >= 13;
```

Output:

```
INTERNAL Error: Failed to bind column reference "k" [0.1] (bindings: {#[21.0]})
```

Expected: `0`.

### Three ingredients, each individually required

Change any one and the query returns `0`. Measured individually on the commit above:

```
baseline (stock)                       -> INTERNAL Error: Failed to bind column reference "k" [0.1] (bindings: {#[21.0]})
SET disabled_optimizers='join_order'      -> 0
SET disabled_optimizers='filter_pushdown' -> 0
ANTI JOIN t7  ->  JOIN t7              -> 0
ANTI JOIN t7  ->  SEMI JOIN t7         -> 0
count(DISTINCT a0.k)  ->  count(*)     -> 0
SET threads=1                          -> INTERNAL Error   (not parallelism-dependent)
```

Any column works — `count(DISTINCT a0.g)` fails the same way.

The fault is at plan time, not execution: `EXPLAIN` alone on the query raises the
identical error.

### The same defect without the join-order optimizer

A wider form fails **even with `join_order` disabled**, with a different binding:

```
INTERNAL Error: Failed to bind column reference "id" [3.1] (bindings: {#[7.0]})
```

That reproducer is 11 joins over 12 tables and would not reduce further — all 11
joins are required. I can attach it; it is `repro-no-join-order.sql` in my notes.
Its existence is why I would not describe this as "the join-order optimizer is
broken": it looks more like a column binding that is not maintained across plan
rewrites generally.


### OS:

Ubuntu 22.04.2 LTS, x86_64 (Linux 5.15.0-187-generic)

### DuckDB Version:

Built from source at `549c3c83fbefedd5fdf5426e8dbeaa4dc8fc56f2` on the `v2.0-cyanoptera` branch (DuckDB's default branch), 2026-09-21. Also reproduces on `81bc275dd6` (2026-09-10) and `ace2451f52` (2026-09-21).

### DuckDB Client:

CLI (`build/release/duckdb`), in-memory database

### Hardware:

_No response_

### Full Name:

Ke Han

### Affiliation:

Purdue University

- [x] Yes, I have

### Did you include all code required to reproduce the issue?

- [x] Yes, I have

Yes

title: Nested joins on d_date_sk = ss_sold_date_sk + k planned as cross product + filter (filter_pullup + join_order lose the equi-join); the flat form plans fine
body:
### What happens?

A chain of INNER JOINs nested as subqueries, each joining the same dimension table on an equality with an arithmetic expression over the same fact column (`d.d_date_sk = ss_sold_date_sk + k`, a different `k` per level), is planned with the innermost join as a **CROSS PRODUCT + FILTER** instead of a hash join. The flat form of the same query (all joins at one level) plans as hash joins, and so does the nested form with `SET disabled_optimizers = 'filter_pullup'` or with the optimizer disabled altogether, so the binder builds the right comparison join and the pullup/pushdown + join-order round trip loses it. With more nesting levels each additional level becomes another cross product (6 levels: 2 hash joins, 4 cross products).

Results are identical (18866 rows for both forms below); only the plan differs. On a real workload (TPC-DS-shaped, `store_sales` joined to `date_dim` as `d1`, then `date_dim` again on `d1.d_date_sk + 30 / + 7 / + 14 / + 21`, rendered as nested subqueries by an engine that generates SQL) the cross products are over 10^5 x 10^5-row inputs and the statement does not finish in 300 s, where the hash-join plan takes 0.07 s.

### To Reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE ss AS SELECT range % 365 AS ss_sold_date_sk, range AS ss_item_sk FROM range(20000);
CREATE TABLE dd AS SELECT range AS d_date_sk, range AS d_date FROM range(365);

EXPLAIN SELECT count(*)
FROM dd d3
JOIN (SELECT * FROM dd d2
      JOIN (SELECT * FROM dd d1 JOIN ss ON d1.d_date_sk = ss.ss_sold_date_sk + 7) a
      ON d2.d_date_sk = a.ss_sold_date_sk + 14) b
ON d3.d_date_sk = b.ss_sold_date_sk + 21;
```

gives (trimmed)

```
HASH_JOIN  (ss_sold_date_sk + 21) = d_date_sk            ~6,460,187 rows
  HASH_JOIN  (ss_sold_date_sk + 14) = d_date_sk          ~6,867,268 rows
    PROJECTION                                            ~7,300,000 rows
      FILTER  d_date_sk = (ss_sold_date_sk + 7)           ~7,300,000 rows
        CROSS_PRODUCT                                     (20,000 x 365)
          SEQ_SCAN ss
          SEQ_SCAN dd
    SEQ_SCAN dd
  SEQ_SCAN dd
```

The same query written flat,

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT count(*) FROM ss
JOIN dd d1 ON d1.d_date_sk = ss.ss_sold_date_sk + 7
JOIN dd d2 ON d2.d_date_sk = ss.ss_sold_date_sk + 14
JOIN dd d3 ON d3.d_date_sk = ss.ss_sold_date_sk + 21;
```

is three hash joins. Variations on the nested form:

| | plan |
|---|---|
| as above | 2 hash joins, 1 cross product + filter |
| `SET disabled_optimizers = 'filter_pullup'` | 3 hash joins |
| `SET disabled_optimizers = 'join_order'` | 1 hash join, 2 cross products |
| `PRAGMA disable_optimizer` | 3 hash joins (the binder's comparison joins) |
| conditions replaced by plain column equalities (`d_date_sk = ss_sold_date_sk` at every level) | 3 hash joins |
| the same three levels as chained CTEs instead of subqueries | 2 hash joins, 1 cross product + filter |
| six levels (`+ 7 ... + 42`) | 2 hash joins, 4 cross products |

So filter pullup lifts the join conditions out of the nested inner joins and the join-order optimizer re-forms all but the innermost (with more levels, all but two) when the conditions are equalities between a column and an arithmetic expression over the same column of the other side.

### OS:

Linux (Ubuntu, aarch64)

### DuckDB Version:

v2.1.0-dev84915 (3b3312a963); also v2.0.0-dev86784 (57c755a991)

### DuckDB Client:

CLI

### Hardware:

### Affiliation:

title: Parquet reader truncates INT96 timestamps to microseconds; no way to read their nanosecond part
body:
### What happens?

`read_parquet` types every INT96 column as `TIMESTAMP` (microseconds), so the sub-microsecond digits the file stores are silently dropped. INT96 stores a Julian day plus nanoseconds of the day, and it is still what Spark, Hive, Impala and SQL Server (`CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE AS SELECT` with `datetime2(7)` / `time(7)`) write by default, so round-tripping their data through DuckDB changes values without a warning.

There is currently no way to opt into the full precision:

- casting the column to `TIMESTAMP_NS` happens after the value was already read at microsecond precision;
- the `schema` parameter of `read_parquet` is keyed by field id, which these writers do not emit, and it also casts after the read;
- no setting or `read_parquet` parameter changes how INT96 is typed.

What makes this look like a small gap rather than a design limit: the Parquet extension already has a nanosecond INT96 path. `ImpalaTimestampToTimestampNS` exists in `parquet_timestamp.cpp`, and `column_reader.cpp` creates a `CallbackColumnReader<Int96, timestamp_ns_t, ImpalaTimestampToTimestampNS>` when the column's logical type is `TIMESTAMP_NS`. However, `ParquetReader::DeriveLogicalType` always returns `LogicalType::TIMESTAMP` for `Type::INT96`, so that reader is never reached:

- https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/7e886f44428e90c8379d4d34e2afb866108ff079/extension/parquet/parquet_reader.cpp#L594-L596
- https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/7e886f44428e90c8379d4d34e2afb866108ff079/extension/parquet/column_reader.cpp#L1063-L1064
- https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/7e886f44428e90c8379d4d34e2afb866108ff079/extension/parquet/parquet_timestamp.cpp#L30-L39

By contrast, an INT64 `TIMESTAMP(NANOS)` column is already read as `TIMESTAMP_NS` with all nine digits (see the last step below), so the behaviour differs only by the physical encoding of the same logical value.

Keeping `TIMESTAMP` as the default makes sense: `TIMESTAMP_NS` only covers 1677-09-21 to 2262-04-11, while INT96 files commonly hold values such as `0001-01-01` or `9999-12-31`. A possible opt-in, purely as a suggestion:

- a `read_parquet` option (for example `int96_as := 'timestamp_ns'`) that makes `DeriveLogicalType` return `TIMESTAMP_NS` and so reaches the existing reader, with out-of-range values raising a conversion error; and/or
- `int96_as := 'blob'` exposing the raw 12 bytes, so callers that need the full `0001`-`9999` range at nanosecond precision can decode the value themselves.

### To Reproduce

The file is written with pyarrow, because DuckDB itself writes INT96 only from microsecond timestamps.

```python
import duckdb
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

values = [
    "1970-01-02 00:00:00.000000001",
    "2026-09-16 10:20:30.123456789",
    "2200-12-31 23:59:59.987654321",
]
table = pa.table({"ts": pa.array(values).cast(pa.timestamp("ns"))})
pq.write_table(table, "int96_ns.parquet", use_deprecated_int96_timestamps=True)

print(pq.ParquetFile("int96_ns.parquet").schema.column(0).physical_type)
print(pq.read_table("int96_ns.parquet").column("ts").cast(pa.string()).to_pylist())

con = duckdb.connect()
print(con.sql("DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM read_parquet('int96_ns.parquet')").fetchall())
print(con.sql("SELECT ts::VARCHAR FROM read_parquet('int96_ns.parquet')").fetchall())
print(con.sql("SELECT ts::TIMESTAMP_NS::VARCHAR FROM read_parquet('int96_ns.parquet')").fetchall())

# Contrast: the same value as INT64 TIMESTAMP(NANOS) keeps all nine digits.
pq.write_table(table, "int64_ns.parquet")
print(con.sql("DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM read_parquet('int64_ns.parquet')").fetchall())
print(con.sql("SELECT ts::VARCHAR FROM read_parquet('int64_ns.parquet')").fetchall())
```

Output (identical on 1.5.5 and 2.0.0.dev2609121639):

```
INT96
['1970-01-02 00:00:00.000000001', '2026-09-16 10:20:30.123456789', '2200-12-31 23:59:59.987654321']
[('ts', 'TIMESTAMP', 'YES', None, None, None)]
[('1970-01-02 00:00:00',), ('2026-09-16 10:20:30.123456',), ('2200-12-31 23:59:59.987654',)]
[('1970-01-02 00:00:00',), ('2026-09-16 10:20:30.123456',), ('2200-12-31 23:59:59.987654',)]
[('ts', 'TIMESTAMP_NS', 'YES', None, None, None)]
[('1970-01-02 00:00:00.000000001',), ('2026-09-16 10:20:30.123456789',), ('2200-12-31 23:59:59.987654321',)]
```

pyarrow reads the INT96 file with all nine digits; DuckDB returns six. The same truncation happens with the DuckDB CLI and with files written by SQL Server 2025 CETAS (`datetime2(7)` value `9999-12-31 23:59:59.9999999` reads as `23:59:59.999999`).

title: NewVuln65 Unbounded Type Nesting Depth Causes Stack Overflow Crash
body:
### What happens?

DuckDB enforces a maximum expression depth of 1000 (via `MaxExpressionDepthSetting`) for arithmetic and logical expression chains. However, **no equivalent limit exists for type-definition nesting**. Type constructors `STRUCT(a STRUCT(a STRUCT(...)))`, `MAP(...)`, and `UNION(...)` can be nested to arbitrary depth without any check firing.

The root cause is in `src/parser/peg/transformer/transform_common.cpp` line 56

```cpp
auto array_depth_guard = transformer.StackCheck(array_bounds ? array_bounds->size() : 0);
```

For STRUCT/MAP/UNION/LIST type constructors, `array_bounds` is always null (only explicit multi-dimensional array subscripts like `INT[3][4]` set it), so `StackCheck(0)` is called. The parser depth counter is **never incremented**. Type nesting therefore bypasses the parser guard entirely.

`TypeVisitor::Contains` and `TypeVisitor::VisitReplace` (`src/include/duckdb/common/type_visitor.hpp`) are the secondary site. Both recurse one stack frame per nesting level with no depth parameter. At depth ≥ 5144 on the default 8 MB thread stack, these recursive calls exhaust the stack. The process terminates with `SIGSEGV` (exit 139), crashing the server.

Note the asymmetry

```sql
-- Expression chains (PROTECTED)
SELECT 1+1+1+... (2000 terms)
-- triggers "Parser Error: Max expression depth limit of 1000 exceeded"

-- Type nesting (NOT PROTECTED)
SELECT typeof(CAST(NULL AS STRUCT(a STRUCT(a ... [5200 levels] ... INTEGER))))
-- triggers SIGSEGV (exit 139), server crash
```

### To Reproduce

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# gen_poc.py

DEPTH = 5200

type_str = 'INTEGER'
for _ in range(DEPTH):
    type_str = 'STRUCT(a ' + type_str + ')'

with open('poc.sql', 'w') as f:
    f.write('SELECT typeof(CAST(NULL AS ' + type_str + '))\n')
```

```sh
python3 gen_poc.py
./build/release/duckdb :memory: < poc.sql
# Segmentation fault (core dumped)   exit 139
```

### Relevant code locations

| File | Line | Note |
|------|------|------|
| `src/parser/peg/transformer/transform_common.cpp` | 56 | `StackCheck(0)` for all type constructors, no depth increment |
| `src/include/duckdb/common/type_visitor.hpp` | 86-131 | `TypeVisitor::Contains` / `VisitReplace`, no depth parameter |
| `src/include/duckdb/main/settings.hpp` | ~1908 | `MaxExpressionDepthSetting` default 1000, only covers expressions |
| `src/parser/peg/transformer/transform_expression.cpp` | 613, 778, 1359 | Expressions **do** call `StackCheck(tails->size())` correctly |

Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS, x86_64 (Linux 6.8.0-55-generic)

title: Bug99: Virtual-column cast pushdown OOB in TypePushdown
body:
### What happens?

In `src/optimizer/type_pushdown.cpp`, `PushdownOptimize()` collects cast expressions over scanned columns into a candidate map (`col_to_expr`). When it encounters a virtual pseudo-column such as `filename` (sentinel id `2^63 = COLUMN_IDENTIFIER_FILENAME`), the loop skips the pushdown via `continue` but **does not null out the map entry**, leaving a stale non-null pointer. Because a sibling real-column cast succeeds and sets `any_pushed = true`, the subsequent `CastReplace` pass runs, sees the stale pointer as "eligible", and indexes `LogicalGet::returned_types` — a vector sized for physical columns only — at position `2^63`, producing an INTERNAL Error / OOB vector access that crashes the process.


### To Reproduce

This is triggered by pure SQL; no external tools or special configuration are needed.

```sql
-- Step 1: create a small CSV file
COPY (SELECT 42 AS col1) TO '/tmp/vuln001_test.csv' (HEADER false);

-- Step 2: trigger the bug - cast both a real column and the virtual 'filename' column
-- NOTE: CAST(filename AS BIGINT) is required; CAST(filename AS VARCHAR) does not trigger.
```

title: Constant-folding a literal cast to VARIANT that overflows silently returns a wrong result instead of erroring
body:
### What happens?

Casting a constant/literal struct value to VARIANT that would produce an encoded row exceeding internal size limits silently returns an incorrect result under default optimizer settings, instead of raising an error. The error is only raised correctly when the optimizer's constant-folding pass is disabled, or when the input comes from a table instead of a literal.

The underlying overflow check itself works correctly (see #25181). This issue is specifically about the check being silently skipped for literal/constant expressions.

As far as I traced it: `ExpressionExecutor::TryEvaluateScalar` (`src/execution/expression_executor.cpp`) is used by `ConstantFoldingRule::Apply` to trial-evaluate constant expressions, and deliberately catches every exception except `InternalException` so a folding attempt that wouldn't actually be reached at runtime (e.g. inside an unreached `CASE` branch) doesn't spuriously fail the query. After a failed fold, the expression should still be evaluated for real at execution time, the same way the division/cast examples above are, but for this VARIANT case that re-evaluation doesn't appear to happen, or its error is lost somewhere. This may be related to the VARIANT cast's "shredded" fast path (`TryToShreddedCast` in `src/function/cast/variant/to_variant.cpp`), which defers the actual byte-encoding of the value until later, when it's flattened/unshredded — but I did not fully trace why that deferred path's error doesn't propagate.

### To Reproduce

Query:
```sql
-- Encoded row size intentionally exceeds 
-- what a VARIANT can represent (UINT32_MAX bytes)
SELECT CAST({'a': repeat('a', 2147483647), 'b': repeat('b', 2147483647), 'c': repeat('c', 2)} AS VARIANT) IS NOT NULL;
```

Expected output: an `Invalid Input Error`.

Actual output: `true`

---

Query:
```sql
-- Disabling constant folding produces the 
-- expected error for the identical query:
SET disabled_optimizers='expression_rewriter';
SELECT CAST({'a': repeat('a', 2147483647), 'b': repeat('b', 2147483647), 'c': repeat('c', 2)} AS VARIANT) IS NOT NULL;
```
Expected = Actual output:
```
Invalid Input Error: Cannot convert value to VARIANT: encoded row size exceeds the maximum supported 4294967295 bytes
```

---

```sql
-- The same query with table-sourced (non-literal) input also 
-- raises the error correctly under default settings:
CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT repeat('a', 2147483647) a, repeat('b', 2147483647) b, repeat('c', 2) c;
SELECT CAST({'a': a, 'b': b, 'c': c} AS VARIANT) IS NOT NULL FROM t;
```
Expected = Actual output:
```
Invalid Input Error: Cannot convert value to VARIANT: encoded row size exceeds the maximum supported 4294967295 bytes
```

title: SIGSEGV when executing an ASOF join with a non-comparison condition
body:
### What happens?

Executing an ASOF join whose `ON` clause contains a non-comparison conjunct crashes with SIGSEGV when the optimizer is disabled. `EXPLAIN` of the same query works, and with the optimizer enabled the query runs fine - the crash only happens when a query is actually executed under `SET debug_disable_optimizer=true`. I hit this while testing #26292, whose disable_optimizer CI run surfaces it through a new ASOF join test.

The crash is in the ASOF nested-loop planning path added by #16218: `PlanAsOfLoopJoin` estimates the cardinality of the join subtree after its children were already planned, and planning a child scan consumes its bind data, so the estimate dereferences a null bind data pointer in `TableScanCardinality`. The table contents and types do not matter - any non-comparison condition (e.g. an `IN` list) triggers it.

### To Reproduce

```sql
SET debug_disable_optimizer=true;
CREATE TABLE a_t AS SELECT (range % 3)::INTEGER AS k, ['sad', 'ok', 'happy'][1 + range % 3] AS m, range::INTEGER AS t FROM range(12);
CREATE TABLE b_t AS SELECT (range % 3)::INTEGER AS k, range::INTEGER AS t FROM range(12);
SELECT count(*)
FROM a_t ASOF JOIN b_t
    ON a_t.k = b_t.k AND a_t.t >= b_t.t AND a_t.m IN ('sad', 'ok', 'happy');
```

Output (the process crashes before producing any result):

```text
zsh: segmentation fault  duckdb < repro.sql
```

The crash stack (from a reldebug build), showing the null bind data reaching the scan's cardinality callback:

```text
* frame #0: duckdb::TableScanCardinality(context=..., bind_data_p=0x0000000000000000) at table_scan.cpp:1133
    frame #1: duckdb::LogicalGet::EstimateCardinality at logical_get.cpp:310
    frame #3: duckdb::LogicalOperator::EstimateCardinality
    frame #4: duckdb::PhysicalPlanGenerator::PlanAsOfLoopJoin at plan_asof_join.cpp:259
    frame #5: duckdb::PhysicalPlanGenerator::PlanAsOfJoin at plan_asof_join.cpp:357
```

Observations that pin it down:

- Without the non-comparison conjunct (`a_t.m IN (...)` removed) the query plans and runs fine.
- `EXPLAIN` of the crashing query does not crash - with the optimizer disabled, nothing caches an estimate on the operators, which is exactly the state in which the post-planning estimate touches the consumed bind data.
- With the optimizer enabled (default) the query also runs fine, because the statistics propagation has already cached cardinalities on every operator.

title: HTTP logging prints Authorization and x-amz-security-token in cleartext; on v2.0 the same rows never reach duckdb_logs() and enable_http_logging is silently inert
body:
### What happens?

Two related defects in HTTP logging.

(A) Credentials are printed in cleartext. Enabling HTTP logging emits every request header, including
    `Authorization: AWS4-HMAC-SHA256 Credential=..., Signature=...` and the full
    `x-amz-security-token` STS session token. Anyone pasting a log into an issue, a chat, or an AI
    agent transcript has published live credentials. We had to treat one session token as burned.

    Which path leaks is version-dependent - measured on one identical query, counting lines
    containing a credential header and distinct Signature= values:

      engine              SET enable_http_logging = true    CALL enable_logging('HTTP')
      v1.4.3              53 header lines / 53 signatures    0 (emits no HTTP rows)
      v1.5.5              79 / 79                            79 / 79
      v2.0.0-alpha41533   0 - accepted but logs nothing      33 / 33

    So this is not a legacy-only problem: the current 2.0 alpha still prints credentials, via the
    newer API. (duckdb/unity_catalog#68 shows the same for a Bearer token.)

    Ask: redact by default - Authorization, x-amz-security-token, Proxy-Authorization, and any header
    whose name contains token/secret/key - with an explicit opt-in for the raw value.

(B) On v2.0 the HTTP log rows are unreachable from SQL. `CALL enable_logging()` or

title: list_reduce can use column values from another row
body:
### What happens?

Using `list_reduce` with a constant initial value and a column reference inside the lambda can return the wrong result when the lists have different lengths. The lambda can read the column value from another row. With a filtered input, it can also fail with an INTERNAL Error.


### To Reproduce


```sql
SELECT v, list_reduce(l, lambda acc, x: acc + x + v, 0) AS result
FROM (VALUES ([1], 10), ([1, 2], 30)) t(l, v);
```

Actual result:

```text
v   result
10  11
30  43
```

The second result should be `63`: `(0 + 1 + 30) + 2 + 30`. Instead, the last step uses `10` from the first row.

Adding a filter can also produce an INTERNAL Error:

```sql
SELECT v, list_reduce(l, lambda acc, x: acc + x + v, 0) AS result
FROM (VALUES ([], 0), ([1], 10), ([1, 2], 30)) t(l, v)
WHERE v > 0;
```

```text
INTERNAL Error: DataChunk::SetChildCardinality - vector has size 2 but expected size 1 - and cannot change vector size because it is not a flat or constant vector
```

title: Unexpected results when comparing a LIST column
body:
### What happens?

*Found by an automated fuzzing/triage agent; the repro is verified, but the analysis may be wrong.*

In a single LIST column, two identical values compared against the same constant return different answers. With rows `[]`, `[-2, -1]`, `[-2, -1]`, the predicate `c > [0]` evaluates to `false`, `false`, `true` — the two `[-2, -1]` rows hold the same value, so whichever answer is right, they cannot differ from each other. The same happens to `list_sort(c) = c`, where two identical `[-1823031693]` rows evaluate to `true` and `false`.

It bisects to `53b8c9c41ed086951f697955979829b70ccfdeaf` (PR #24162, "Internal #5184: Nested Equality", landed 2026-07-27), verified present at the culprit and absent at its parent. The commit is part of the ongoing nested-comparison rework, so this may already be known or already covered by work in flight--please close it if so.


### To Reproduce

```sql
SELECT c, c > [0] AS gt FROM (VALUES ([]::INTEGER[]), ([-2, -1]), ([-2, -1])) v(c);
-- Expected: the two [-2, -1] rows agree
-- Actual:   false, false, true

SELECT c, list_sort(c) = c AS eq FROM (VALUES ([0]), ([0]), ([0]), ([1, NULL, 2]), ([-1823031693]), ([1, NULL, 2]), ([-1823031693])) v(c);
-- Expected: the two [-1823031693] rows agree
-- Actual:   true, true, true, false, true, false, false
```

A filter then splits the identical rows: with a third row holding the same value as the second, one is kept and the other is not, and the complementary filter picks up exactly the one that was dropped.

```sql
CREATE TABLE t0(c0 INTEGER[], c1 INT);
INSERT INTO t0 VALUES ([], 1), ([-2, -1], 2), ([-2, -1], 3);

SELECT c1 FROM t0 WHERE NOT (c0 > [0]) ORDER BY c1;
-- Expected: rows 2 and 3 are both present or both absent
-- Actual:   1, 2

SELECT c1 FROM t0 WHERE (c0 > [0]) ORDER BY c1;
-- Actual:   3
```

title: NewVuln23 struct_contains / struct_position Returns Wrong Result for Mixed Numeric Type Structs
body:
### What happens?

`StructContainsBind()` (`src/function/scalar/struct/struct_contains.cpp`) constructs an aliased struct type for binding by copying child types from the input struct. When the struct contains members of mixed numeric types (e.g., `FLOAT` and `DOUBLE`), the aliasing operation assigns the wrong physical type to each member, causing the subsequent element-wise comparison to mismatch a `FLOAT` member is compared as if it were a `DOUBLE`, producing a false negative. `struct_contains(ROW(1.0  FLOAT, 2.0  DOUBLE), 1.0  FLOAT)` returns `false` and `struct_position` returns `NULL` instead of `1`.

### To Reproduce

```sql
SELECT struct_contains(ROW(1.0::FLOAT, 2.0::DOUBLE), 1.0::FLOAT) AS result;
-- Expected: true
-- Got:      false

SELECT struct_position(ROW(1.0::FLOAT, 2.0::DOUBLE), 1.0::FLOAT) AS pos;
-- Expected: 1
-- Got:      NULL
```

title: ManualVuln27 Window Clause Reference Lost When Any Subquery Precedes OVER Clause in SELECT List
body:
### What happens?

`FinalizeSimpleSelectTrampoline` (`src/parser/peg/transformer/transform_select.cpp`, line 310) unconditionally calls `transformer.window_clauses.clear()` at the end of every SELECT finalization, including for inner subqueries. The `window_clauses` map is a flat shared field on the `PEGTransformer` instance rather than a properly scoped stack.

In the trampoline execution model, select-list items are pushed onto a processing stack so the first item in the list is processed first. When a subquery appears as the first (or any earlier) item in the outer SELECT list, the trampoline finalizes that inner SELECT completely, calling `window_clauses.clear()` and erasing the outer SELECT's registered window names. When the trampoline then processes any later select-list expression that references the outer window via a named `OVER <name>` clause, `GetWindowClause` (`src/parser/peg/transformer/peg_transformer.cpp`, line 371) fails to find the name and throws `ParserException("window %s does not exist", window_name)`.

The invariant violated is that window clause registrations must remain visible for the duration of the SELECT that owns them, not be cleared by the finalization of any inner SELECT encountered in the same traversal.

The same root cause pattern as the `stored_cte_map` stack-use-after-return (issue 25173) applies here: a piece of per-SELECT parser state (`window_clauses`) is stored flat on the transformer without scope-stack discipline, so finalization of a nested SELECT corrupts the enclosing SELECT's state.

### To Reproduce

Reproducible directly via plain SQL from the DuckDB CLI client, no external file or script required.

SQL script (`manual27_window_clause_lost_by_subquery.sql`):

```sql
SELECT (SELECT 1), sum(1) OVER w WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY 1)
```

Trigger output:

```
Parser Error: window "w" does not exist
```

+query II
+SELECT (SELECT 1), sum(1) OVER w WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY 1)
+----
+1	1
+
+query II
+SELECT sum(1) OVER w, (SELECT 1) WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY 1)
+----

+

+query I
+SELECT a FROM (SELECT 1) t(a) WINDOW w AS () QUALIFY sum(a) OVER w > 0
+----
+1
+
+query I
+SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT * FROM range(3) WHERE (SELECT true) WINDOW w AS () QUALIFY sum(1) OVER w > 0)
+----
+3
+

+query III

+FROM range(3) t(i)
+WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY i ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
+ORDER BY 3

+1	2	1
+1	2	3

+query II
+SELECT sum(1) OVER w, (SELECT sum(2) OVER w WINDOW w AS ()) WINDOW w AS ()
+----
+1	2
+
+query II
+SELECT (SELECT sum(2) OVER w WINDOW w AS ()), sum(1) OVER w WINDOW w AS ()
+----
+2	1
+

+query II

+FROM range(2) t(j)
+WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY j ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
+ORDER BY 2
+----
+3	0
+3	1

+statement error

+statement error
+SELECT * FROM (SELECT sum(1) OVER w) WINDOW w AS ()

+statement error

title: ManualVuln3 approx_top_k() Import State Accepts Zero-Count Entries, Causing Assertion Failure in Debug and Silent Result Corruption in Release
body:
### What happens?

`ApproxTopKImportState` (`extension/core_functions/aggregate/holistic/approx_top_k.cpp` lines 478 to 548) validates the structural shape of an imported aggregate state: `value_entries[i].length > target.capacity` (line 516) guards against an over-sized values list, and `filter_entries[i].length != target.filter.size()` guards against a mis-sized filter array. However, it does not validate the `count` field of each value entry. At line 540, the import stores the user-supplied counter directly without any lower-bound check:

```cpp
val.count = count_data[idx];
```

Every path that builds an `InternalApproxTopKState` during normal aggregation maintains the invariant `val.count > 0` for every tracked entry. `InternalApproxTopKState::Verify()` (lines 153 to 175) asserts this invariant for every stored value. `ApproxTopKFinalize` (line 371) asserts it again before materialising each result entry. Both assertions are guarded by `#ifdef DEBUG` and `D_ASSERT`, so they are active checks in debug builds and silent no-ops in release.

Because the import path calls `target.Verify()` at line 545 unconditionally, a crafted state with any value whose `count == 0` aborts the process in a debug build via `D_ASSERT(val.count > 0)`. In a release build the assertion is suppressed. The zero-count entry is accepted into the state and propagates to `Finalize`, which includes it in the output list. The result contains an item reported as occurring zero times, which the calling application would never observe under normal data, constituting silent logical corruption.

The root cause is the same trust-boundary gap identified in GitHub issue #24279 for `approximate_quantile`: the import callback for a stateful aggregate function must independently re-validate every field invariant of the imported state, because external callers using `to_aggregate_state` can supply arbitrary values that the normal aggregation path would never produce.

Only two aggregate functions in the codebase register an import state callback. `approximate_quantile` was fixed in PR #24425 by adding a cross-validation check between `count` and the centroids list. `approx_top_k` received length and null checks but the `count > 0` invariant is enforced only by `D_ASSERT`, leaving it bypassable through the import path.


### To Reproduce

Reproducible directly via plain SQL from the DuckDB CLI client, no external file or script required. The debug build exposes the assertion failure. The release build exposes the silent data corruption.

SQL script (`vuln_approx_top_k_zero_count.sql`):

```sql
-- Craft a malicious state where one entry has count = 0.
-- k=2, filter size = NextPowerOfTwo(2*3*8) = 64, one value 'evil' with count=0.
SELECT finalize(
    to_aggregate_state(
        {'k': 2::UBIGINT, 'values': [{'value': 'evil', 'count': 0::UBIGINT}], 'filter': list_apply(range(64), lambda x: 0::UBIGINT)},
        'approx_top_k',
        ['VARCHAR', 'BIGINT'],
        [NULL, 2]
    )
) AS result;
-- Expected: InvalidInputException (missing count > 0 validation)
-- Actual debug: INTERNAL Error assertion failure at approx_top_k.cpp:162
-- Actual release: returns ['evil'] with a zero-count entry, silent data corruption
```

Trigger output (debug build):

```
INTERNAL Error: Assertion triggered in file "approx_top_k.cpp" on line 162: val.count > 0

./duckdb(+0x2790a79f) [approx_top_k.cpp:545 ApproxTopKImportState<HistogramStringFunctor>]
...
```

title: ManualVuln24 Null Pointer Dereference in ParseOrderBys via Non-VARCHAR 'order' Field in to_aggregate_state ORDER BY Spec
body:
### What happens?

In `ParseOrderBys` (`src/function/scalar/system/aggregate_export.cpp`, line 694), the `order` field is extracted from a user-supplied `{column, order}` struct by name, with only a NULL-value guard at line 684. The code then passes `order` directly to `StringValue::Get(order)` without first checking that `order.type().id() == LogicalTypeId::VARCHAR`. `StringValue::Get` at `src/common/types/value.cpp:1954` guards with `D_ASSERT(value.type().InternalType() == PhysicalType::VARCHAR)` (debug-only) and `D_ASSERT(value.value_info_)` (debug-only), then calls `value.value_info_->Get<StringValueInfo>().GetString()`. For non-VARCHAR primitive values such as INTEGER, `value.value_info_` is a null `shared_ptr` because primitive types store their data in the union member rather than in the heap-allocated extra-info object. In release builds both asserts are removed, and DuckDB's custom `shared_ptr` null-check then fires and throws `INTERNAL Error: Attempted to dereference shared_ptr that is NULL`, crashing any session that calls `to_aggregate_state` with a non-VARCHAR order-modifier field. The vulnerability is reachable from pure SQL with no external files or special configuration.

### To Reproduce

Reproducible directly via plain SQL from the DuckDB CLI client, no external file or script required.

SQL script (`manual24_nullderef.sql`):

```sql
SELECT to_aggregate_state([{'v0': 'a'}], 'string_agg', ['VARCHAR'], NULL, [{'column': 0, 'order': 42}]);
```

```cpp
//! True iff the build subtree funnels multiple producer pipelines into one sink (UNION ALL, recursive CTE),
//! breaking the "decide layout once on the first chunk" contract. Conservative: may over-exclude, never misses one.
static bool BuildSideHasMultipleSources(const PhysicalOperator &op) {
	if (op.type == PhysicalOperatorType::UNION || op.type == PhysicalOperatorType::RECURSIVE_CTE ||
	    op.type == PhysicalOperatorType::RECURSIVE_KEY_CTE) {
		return true;
	}

        // ***Workaround***
        // Avoids assertion failure and out of memory condition
        //
	// A CTE reference replays chunks produced elsewhere by the CTE definition, which this static walk cannot see
	// through. That definition may itself be a UNION (or otherwise stream differently-sized global dictionaries per
	// chunk), so the "one stable dictionary decided on the first chunk" contract is not guaranteed. Disqualify.
	if (op.type == PhysicalOperatorType::CTE_SCAN || op.type == PhysicalOperatorType::RECURSIVE_CTE_SCAN ||
	    op.type == PhysicalOperatorType::RECURSIVE_RECURRING_CTE_SCAN) {
		return true;
	}
	for (const auto &child : op.children) {
		if (BuildSideHasMultipleSources(child.get())) {
			return true;
		}
	}

	return false;
}
```

title: ManualVuln29 Signed Integer Overflow in ICUCalendarSub via TIMESTAMPTZ Subtraction with INT64_MIN Interval Micros
body:
### What happens?

`ICUCalendarSub::Operation(timestamp_tz_t timestamp, interval_t interval, TZCalendar &calendar)` in `extension/icu/icu-dateadd.cpp` at line 136 constructs a negated interval with:

```cpp
const interval_t negated {-interval.months, -interval.days, -interval.micros};
```

This negates `interval.micros` (type `int64_t`) without any bounds check. When `interval.micros` equals `INT64_MIN` (-9223372036854775808), the negation `-interval.micros` overflows a signed 64-bit integer, which is undefined behavior in C++ and aborts the process under UBSan.

The root cause mirrors issue #25084: `SubtractTimeOperator::Operation` negated `right.micros` (int64_t) without guarding against INT64_MIN. PR #25138 fixed that path and also fixed `Interval::Invert`. However `ICUCalendarSub` implements `TIMESTAMPTZ - INTERVAL` independently and bypasses `Interval::Invert` entirely, so those guards give no protection here.

An interval literal whose microsecond fields sum to exactly INT64_MIN parses successfully because `Interval::FromCString` only overflow-checks the addition of its individual terms, not the final negation performed later in `ICUCalendarSub`. The two-term literal `-4611686018427387904 microseconds -4611686018427387904 microseconds` parses to `interval.micros = -4611686018427387904 + -4611686018427387904 = -9223372036854775808 = INT64_MIN`.

ManualVuln28 documents the INT32_MIN overflow for `interval.months` and `interval.days` at the same line. This entry documents the INT64_MIN overflow for `interval.micros` at column 62 of the same line.

### To Reproduce

Reproducible directly via plain SQL from the DuckDB CLI client, no external file or script required.

SQL script (`manual29_icu_timestamptz_interval_micros_overflow.sql`):

```sql
SELECT TIMESTAMPTZ '2024-01-01 12:00:00+00' - INTERVAL '-4611686018427387904 microseconds -4611686018427387904 microseconds'
```

Trigger output:

```
.../extension/icu/icu-dateadd.cpp:136:62: runtime error: negation of -9223372036854775808 cannot be represented in type 'long int'; cast to an unsigned type to negate this value to itself
```

title: ManualVuln25 Null Dereference in PIVOT IN List Binding via Zero-Argument row() Function
body:
### What happens?

In `TransformPivotInList` (`src/parser/peg/transformer/transform_select.cpp`, lines 469-497), the FUNCTION case checks whether the function name is "row" and then iterates over its child arguments. When `row()` is called with zero arguments, the loop body never executes and the function returns `true`, signaling that the expression was fully transformed into concrete values. However, no values were actually appended to `pivot_entry.values`.

In `TransformPivotTargetList` (lines 1460-1474 of the same file), the return value `true` causes the branch that assigns `pivot_entry.expr = std::move(target)` to be skipped. As a result, the entry is pushed into the result vector with both `values` empty and `expr` holding a null `unique_ptr<ParsedExpression>`.

In `Binder::BindPivot` (`src/planner/binder/tableref/bind_pivot.cpp`, around line 618), the binder iterates all `PivotColumnEntry` objects in each `PivotColumn`. For any entry where `pivot_entry.values.empty()` is true it calls `BindPivotInList(pivot_entry.expr, pivot_entry.values, *this)`.
